paper.title: Primary cilia connect epithelial mesenchymal plasticity with anoikis resistance and cancer stemness.
paper.abstract: Metastatic dissemination requires carcinoma cells to coordinate reversible changes in epithelial identity with survival following extracellular matrix detachment and retention of tumor-initiating capacity. However, the mechanisms integrating epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity (EMP), anoikis resistance, and cancer stemness remain incompletely defined. Primary cilia are spatially restricted signaling compartments whose assembly and function vary with cell state, tumor lineage, and pathway context. This review evaluates how primary cilia may connect these metastatic adaptations by organizing responses to microenvironmental cues. Evidence from mammary epithelial and breast cancer models links selected EMP states to increased ciliogenesis and to Hedgehog-GLI or cilium-dependent GLIS2 signaling, which may support stem-like properties and treatment resistance. Ciliary signaling can also intersect with adhesion, cytoskeletal, and pro-survival pathways involved in survival after detachment. However, these downstream networks are not specific to primary cilia, and direct evidence that ciliary signaling causes anoikis resistance remains limited. Hypoxia, matrix stiffness, and receptor-mediated signals may further modify ciliary function and cellular plasticity, but their effects are tumor- and model-dependent. Overall, primary cilia should be viewed as context-dependent organizers rather than universal drivers of metastatic behavior. Future studies should define ciliary status alongside EMP state, anchorage-independent survival, and functional stemness to determine when cilia constrain tumor progression, support malignant signaling, or provide therapeutically actionable dependencies.
paper.full_text:
Introduction
Primary cilia are solitary, microtubule-based projections that extend from the surface of many mammalian cells. Built from a basal body and an axonemal microtubule core, they provide a specialized membrane compartment where selected receptors, trafficking proteins, and signaling molecules are concentrated [1–4]. Although they are often described as sensory organelles, their function can be understood as context-dependent signal organization, not only passive signal reception. This architecture allows extracellular mechanical and biochemical cues to be interpreted in a spatially restricted manner.

Several cancer-relevant pathways intersect with ciliary biology. The relationship is strongest for Hedgehog (Hh) signaling, in which PTCH1 and SMO trafficking, together with GLI processing, depend closely on the ciliary compartment in many vertebrate cells [5, 6]. Wnt/β-catenin and Notch signaling, together with receptor tyrosine kinase pathways such as the PDGF-AA–PDGFRα and IGF-1–IGF1R axes, have also been linked to primary cilia; however, these relationships vary with cell type, tumor lineage, and pathway state [7–12]. Downstream survival modules may also intersect with ciliary signaling without being primary cilium-specific. These include phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/AKT) and mitogen-activated protein kinase/extracellular signal-regulated kinase (MAPK/ERK). In cancer, cilia can therefore support oncogenic signaling in selected settings, whereas ciliary loss or reduced ciliogenesis has been associated with tumor progression in others [7, 8].

Most cancer deaths are related to metastatic disease, but dissemination is not driven by one cellular program alone. In many carcinomas, a tumor cell that leaves an epithelial lesion must loosen cell-cell contacts, remodel its cytoskeleton, detach from the extracellular matrix (ECM), and survive while displaced from its original tissue environment [13]. These changes are often described in relation to epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), but epithelial–mesenchymal plasticity (EMP) is a more suitable framework for this review because it emphasizes reversible transitions among multiple epithelial, hybrid, and mesenchymal states rather than reducing this process to a binary shift between fixed endpoints [14–18]. These states are not merely combinations of markers: in vivo phenotypic profiling and lineage-tracing studies show that they differ in cellular plasticity, invasiveness, metastatic competence, and treatment response [17, 18]. Partial or hybrid states may retain epithelial cell–cell adhesion while acquiring mesenchymal motility and stress tolerance, allowing tumor cells to adapt across successive stages of dissemination. In this setting, cytoskeletal remodeling and reduced dependence on matrix attachment are closely related to anoikis resistance, because detached cells must suppress apoptotic signaling while maintaining sufficient survival pathway activity [14–16, 19–23].

Anoikis resistance is also linked to stem-like tumor cell states, although this relationship is not uniform across all cancers. Cancer stem cells (CSCs), or tumor cells with stem-like properties, are associated with self-renewal, tumor-initiating capacity, therapy tolerance, and increased metastatic potential [24–27]. Accordingly, stemness should be assessed functionally rather than inferred from a universal marker panel, because marker expression varies by tumor type and experimental model [24–27]. Stem-like states are maintained by developmental signaling, cellular plasticity, and cues from the tumor microenvironment (TME) [28]. Several microenvironmental conditions relevant to detachment survival and cellular plasticity may intersect with ciliary biology. Hypoxia and matrix stiffness can alter ciliary properties in defined cellular models [29, 30], whereas TGF-β, PDGF-AA, and IGF-1 provide examples of soluble mediators whose receptor signaling can be spatially coordinated at or near the ciliary compartment [11, 12, 31]. Whether ECM detachment itself directly remodels primary cilia remains unclear. Primary cilia may therefore act as one context-dependent site where microenvironmental signals and plasticity-related pathways intersect.

In this review, we discuss how primary cilia may connect EMP with anoikis resistance and cancer stemness. We first summarize core ciliary biology and major cilia-associated signaling pathways, then examine how these pathways intersect with adhesion remodeling, survival signaling, and stem-like states during metastatic dissemination. We also consider TME regulation and therapeutic approaches involving cilia-associated structures, ciliogenesis-related regulators, and downstream signaling pathways. Throughout the review, we distinguish established cilia-dependent mechanisms from tumor-specific findings and emerging links that require further validation.

Primary cilia as context-dependent signaling compartments in cancer
Primary cilia are now recognized as specialized signaling organelles rather than vestigial cellular structures. They organize selected receptors, trafficking machinery, and signaling proteins within a restricted membrane compartment, allowing extracellular cues to be interpreted in a spatially regulated manner [1, 7, 8]. In cancer, this function should not be viewed as a uniform driver of malignant progression. Instead, primary cilia appear to have tumor-type- and pathway-dependent roles. In some settings, intact cilia support cilia-dependent signaling, whereas in others, reduced ciliogenesis or ciliary loss may alter downstream pathways through non-canonical mechanisms [7, 8]. This context dependence is particularly relevant when considering the links between primary cilia, CSC-like states, epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, and anoikis resistance.

The Hh pathway remains the clearest example of a cilia-dependent signaling pathway with relevance to cancer. Mechanistically, primary cilia provide an important compartment for PTCH1 and SMO trafficking and for GLI processing during canonical Hh signaling [5–6, 32, 33]. Under basal conditions, PTCH1 restrains SMO activity; after ligand engagement, SMO accumulates in the ciliary compartment and promotes GLI-dependent transcriptional output. This mechanism helps explain why Hh signaling is often discussed together with ciliary biology. However, the relationship between ciliary status and Hh pathway output is not identical across tumor types. In breast cancer, inhibition of ciliogenesis has been reported to promote Hh signaling rather than suppress it. This effect has been described in triple-negative breast cancer, where ciliary loss was associated with activation of a Hh-TGFA signaling loop and tumor progression [34]. This contrasts with many developmental contexts, in which ciliary trafficking and GLI processing are required for canonical Hh output [5]. These findings support a context-dependent interpretation rather than a simple model in which cilia always promote or always suppress Hh pathway activity.

Wnt/β-catenin signaling is also linked to primary cilia, although this relationship is less direct than that of Hh signaling [35]. In some models, the primary cilium has been proposed to restrain canonical Wnt/β-catenin activity, but the outcome depends on cell lineage, differentiation state, and the mechanism through which ciliogenesis is altered. Melanoma provides one tumor-specific example. In this setting, EZH2-mediated primary cilium deconstruction was reported to increase Wnt/β-catenin signaling and promote a more aggressive phenotype [36]. This observation supports the idea that ciliary loss can affect plasticity-related signaling pathways. At the same time, it should be interpreted as evidence from a defined tumor model, not as a general rule for all cancers.

The relationship between primary cilia and Notch signaling should be treated more cautiously than the relationship between primary cilia and Hh signaling. Notch activation is primarily contact dependent: ligand binding, for example through DLL1, induces proteolytic cleavage of the receptor and releases the Notch intracellular domain (NICD), which then enters the nucleus and regulates transcription with CSL [37]. This core activation process is not centered on the ciliary compartment. Even so, Notch remains relevant to this review because it is involved in cell fate control, stem-like phenotypes, survival, invasion, and tumor microenvironmental interactions in several cancers [37, 38]. More broadly, developmental signaling pathways, including Notch, can contribute to therapy resistance and malignant cell-state regulation in selected contexts [38]. Thus, Notch is best discussed here as a plasticity- and stemness-related pathway that may intersect with ciliary biology in selected settings, rather than as a clearly cilium-dependent pathway.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma provides one example of this more limited type of connection. SOX9 has been reported to regulate cilia-related genes and to participate in developmental signaling programs that include Notch activity [39]. This does not prove a universal cilium-Notch mechanism. Rather, it indicates that ciliary gene expression, lineage state, and developmental signaling can be coordinated in particular tumor contexts. For this reason, the evidence in this section should be weighted by pathway. Canonical Hh signaling has the strongest mechanistic dependence on the primary cilium. Wnt/β-catenin and Notch signaling show more variable relationships with ciliary biology. Among receptor-mediated pathways, ciliary coordination has been demonstrated for PDGF-AA–PDGFRα signaling in quiescent fibroblasts [11] and for IGF-1–IGF1R signaling in fibroblast and epithelial models [12]. TGF-β receptors can localize to the ciliary tip and to endocytic vesicles at the ciliary base, where ligand stimulation promotes SMAD2/3 and ERK1/2 activation [31]. Because these mechanisms have been defined largely in nonmalignant cellular models, they should not be generalized to all tumor contexts. PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK are better described as downstream or intersecting survival modules, not as primary cilium-specific pathways.

Anoikis resistance as a survival requirement during metastatic dissemination
Under physiological conditions, the detachment of epithelial or endothelial cells from the ECM precipitates an immediate apoptotic cell death—a phenomenon termed anoikis. This anchorage-dependency acts as a physiological safeguard, enforcing tissue architecture and precluding the dissemination of detached cells. To colonize distant sites, however, disseminated tumor cells must circumvent this checkpoint [40–43]. The acquisition of anoikis resistance is not a singular event but relies on a concerted molecular reconfiguration: specifically, the remodeling of the integrin-cytoskeleton axis, the constitutive hyperactivation of pro-survival cascades, and the amplification of anti-apoptotic logic.

Bridging the extracellular architecture and the intracellular scaffold, integrins function not merely as adhesive anchors but as mechanochemical transducers that link ECM dynamics to the cytoskeleton [40, 44]. Malignant cells frequently dysregulate this signaling axis to decouple survival from attachment. This process is evident in prostate cancer, where the overexpression of TUBB3 potentiates the αvβ3/focal adhesion kinase (FAK)/Src cascade, effectively insulating cells against anoikis to fuel bone metastasis [45]. A distinct co-option strategy appears in highly metastatic colon carcinoma: even in the void of ECM attachment, integrins α2β1 and α5β1 physically recruit and activate EGFR. This aberrant interaction ignites downstream ERK/AKT survival signals, thereby reducing caspase-3 activation [46]. More broadly, FAK can couple integrin-derived adhesion signals to downstream pro-survival pathways [40, 44]. In the colon cancer model described above, however, the cited study demonstrated direct association of integrins α2β1 and α5β1 with EGFR and the consequent maintenance of ERK/AKT signaling, without establishing FAK as a required intermediary [46].

To evade the metabolic stress of detachment, tumor cells predominantly rely on two canonical survival pathways: the PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK signaling axes [20, 40, 47]. This systemic exploitation is exemplified in prostate malignancy, where Brain-derived neurotrophic factor engages the tropomyosin receptor kinase B receptor—not for neural maintenance, but to ignite an AKT-driven program of invasion and anchorage-independence [48]. Conversely, the therapeutic vulnerability of this network is highlighted by agents like moscatilin, which dismantles anoikis resistance in lung carcinoma specifically by dampening the dual hyperactivity of both the AKT and ERK modules [20, 40]. A receptor-specific connection to ciliary biology is provided by PDGF-AA–PDGFRα signaling. In growth-arrested fibroblasts, PDGFRα localizes to the primary cilium, and ligand stimulation is followed by activation of AKT and MEK1/2–ERK1/2 signaling [11]. However, this mechanism has not been shown to operate in detached tumor cells or to cause anoikis resistance.

The arbitration of cell fate hinges on the balance within the Bcl-2 family, where pro-apoptotic effectors, such as Bax and Bak, are opposed by anti-apoptotic members, such as Bcl-2 and Mcl-1. To enforce anoikis resistance, tumor cells can shift this ratio toward survival. Increased expression of anti-apoptotic proteins such as Bcl-2 and Mcl-1 can reduce the activation of pro-apoptotic effectors and suppress the mitochondrial apoptotic pathway [49]. This molecular regulation is often directed by upstream drivers; for instance, in ovarian carcinoma, the FZD7-TWIST1 axis functions as an upstream regulator, directly modulating Bcl-2 abundance to secure survival during detachment [50].

Anoikis resistance also involves molecular mechanisms beyond canonical signaling pathways. In glioma models, isocucurbitacin B promoted anoikis and suppressed tumor growth by downregulating CAV1 and altering cholesterol-associated survival mechanisms [51]. Parallel to this is a strategy of translational selectivity: metastatic breast cancer cells can use DAP5/eIF3d-dependent selective mRNA translation to sustain specific protein synthesis programs. Increased DAP5 expression has also been associated with poor metastasis-free survival [52]. Yet, these intrinsic adaptations tell only half the story. The TME functions not as a passive backdrop, but as an active source of selective pressure. Through physical and chemical stressors—ranging from hypoxia and acidic pH to matrix stiffness and immune infiltration—the TME can support the development of anoikis resistance [28, 40]. Taken together, these studies establish multiple adhesion, survival, apoptotic, translational, and microenvironmental routes to detachment survival, but they do not demonstrate that primary cilia are required for anoikis resistance. In the present framework, primary cilia are therefore considered candidate organizers of selected upstream signals rather than established components of the anoikis-resistance machinery.

Epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity and remodeling of adhesion, cytoskeleton, and survival signaling
Anoikis resistance should be considered across the EMP continuum rather than as a consequence restricted to complete EMT. Cells in partial or hybrid states can remodel adhesion, cytoskeletal organization, and survival signaling while retaining selected epithelial features, making EMP more informative than a binary EMT model for understanding detachment survival [14–20]. Through this coordinated but state-dependent remodeling, cells occupying distinct EMP states may reduce their susceptibility to the apoptotic stress of detachment without undergoing a uniform or complete mesenchymal conversion [19, 20].

A key molecular feature of EMT is the cadherin switch, characterized by reduced epithelial E-cadherin expression and increased mesenchymal N-cadherin expression [53]. This change can weaken cell-cell adhesion and may contribute to signaling changes that support migration and survival after detachment. In cervical cancer models, loss of miR-525-5p has been reported to promote metastasis and anoikis resistance through the UBE2C/ZEB1/2 axis [54]. The cadherin switch is therefore best treated as a useful readout, not as a complete definition of EMT. Depending on the tumor type and model, reduced E-cadherin may be accompanied by loss of cytokeratins, increased vimentin or fibronectin, and variable induction of SNAIL, SLUG, ZEB, or TWIST. These changes do not always occur together or in a fixed sequence, which is one reason why epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity is a more appropriate framework than a simple epithelial-to-mesenchymal conversion [14, 53, 55, 56]. Importantly, this state dependence also extends to ciliary biology. In mammary epithelial and breast cancer models, EMT programs induced by SNAIL, TWIST, or ZEB1 expression, or by E-cadherin depletion, promoted primary ciliogenesis [57]. Subsequent work showed that EMT programs induced primary ciliogenesis upon entry into intermediate epithelial–mesenchymal states and linked the ciliary compartment to the regulation and functional inactivation of GLIS2 [58]. More recently, analyses of human triple-negative breast cancer biopsies and patient-derived organoids identified quasi-mesenchymal ciliated stem-like cells as a subset of late-hybrid epithelial–mesenchymal cells, indicating that primary ciliogenesis was restricted to selected EMP states in these models rather than uniformly present across the continuum [59].

Adhesion changes are accompanied by remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton, which can support migration, altered cell shape, and survival under detachment stress [19, 20]. The therapeutic potential of targeting this machinery is highlighted in hepatocellular carcinoma, where Catechol acts to inhibit the EGFR-AKT-ERK axis, reducing cytoskeletal changes required for invasion [60]. Ultimately, these structural adaptations are not isolated; they feed into a broader survival network, where EMT-driven signals (via transforming growth factor beta and matrix metalloproteinases) directly recalibrate the apoptotic threshold to favor persistence over death [61]. In this sense, EMP provides a useful framework for linking changes in adhesion and cytoskeletal organization with the survival programs required for anchorage-independent growth. Together, these findings argue against treating ciliogenesis as a uniform consequence of EMT and instead support a state-specific relationship between EMP and primary cilia. However, the evidence remains concentrated in mammary epithelial and breast cancer models, and whether this relationship directly regulates anoikis resistance remains unresolved [57–59].

Cancer stemness and partial epithelial-mesenchymal states in anchorage-independent survival
Cancer stemness is therefore best understood as a context-dependent functional state rather than an invariant cellular identity [24–27, 62–64]. During metastatic dissemination, stemness and anoikis resistance provide complementary but non-equivalent functions: anoikis resistance enables survival after ECM detachment, whereas stemness maintains the capacity for self-renewal and tumor initiation at subsequent sites [24–28]. Developmental pathways such as Wnt/β-catenin, Hh, and Notch can sustain cell-state plasticity and self-renewal, whereas PI3K/AKT and Bcl-2-family signaling can increase stress tolerance and raise the apoptotic threshold. These mechanisms provide potential points of convergence between stemness and detachment survival [38, 49, 65]. Metabolic plasticity may reinforce this overlap: CSC-associated metabolic adaptations support stress and therapy tolerance [66], whereas anoikis-resistant melanoma cells have been shown to shift toward oxidative metabolism using glutamine and fatty acids [67]. These observations indicate convergent stress-adaptation programs but do not establish that all stem-like cells are anoikis-resistant.

The relationship between EMP and stemness is state-dependent rather than monotonic: EMP can facilitate the reversible acquisition and loss of stem-like properties, but stemness does not necessarily increase as cells progress toward a fully mesenchymal phenotype [14–18, 68, 69]. Partial or hybrid states may be particularly relevant because they can retain epithelial adhesion and proliferative competence while acquiring increased motility and stress tolerance, thereby supporting both dissemination and subsequent tumor initiation [15–18, 68, 69]. In colorectal cancer, the Claudin-1–EPHA2 complex provides a tumor-specific example in which adhesion-associated signaling enhances AKT activity and promotes tumor-initiating capacity and chemoresistance [70]; however, the cited study did not directly establish this complex as a mediator of anoikis resistance. In mammary epithelial and breast cancer models, selected EMP states engage primary cilia to support stem-like functions through Hh–GLI signaling or cilium-dependent GLIS2 regulation [57, 58]. Human triple-negative breast cancer data further identify ciliated late-hybrid cells with stem-like and chemoresistant properties [59], although whether these ciliary programs also cause anoikis resistance remains unknown.

Taken together, EMP, anoikis resistance, and cancer stemness should be viewed as overlapping but non-equivalent adaptations. EMP enables reversible cell-state transitions, anoikis resistance allows detached cells to persist, and stemness maintains tumor-initiating capacity after dissemination. Their convergence may therefore be most consequential in plastic tumor cells that survive detachment while retaining tumor-initiating capacity. Primary cilia may organize part of this convergence in selected tumors, but current direct evidence is strongest for the EMP–stemness relationship and remains limited for a causal cilia–anoikis relationship [57–59]. Tumor microenvironmental regulation of ciliary signaling and cancer cell plasticity
Yet, these intrinsic adaptations tell only part of the story. The TME functions not as a passive backdrop, but as an active source of biochemical and physical signals. Through physical and chemical stressors ranging from hypoxia and acidic pH to matrix stiffness and immune infiltration, the TME can support or select for anoikis resistance [28, 40, 71, 72]. Stem-like states are rarely autonomous; they are influenced by signals from the TME, where extrinsic cues shape tumor cell plasticity and survival [28, 40, 73].

This relationship is relevant to primary cilia because cilia are positioned at the cell surface and contain selected receptors, trafficking machinery, and signaling proteins. Within the TME, primary cilia may help cells organize responses to mechanical and biochemical cues [1, 7, 8]. Among soluble mediators, TGF-β is particularly relevant because TGF-β receptors can localize to the ciliary tip and to endocytic vesicles at the ciliary base, where ligand stimulation promotes SMAD2/3 and ERK1/2 activation [31]. PDGF-AA–PDGFRα and IGF-1–IGF1R provide additional receptor-specific examples of signaling spatially coordinated by primary cilia [11, 12]. These mechanisms have been defined mainly in nonmalignant fibroblast and epithelial models and should not be assumed to operate identically in tumors. Hypoxia may influence ciliary biology, whereas matrix stiffness has been shown to alter ciliary length and centriole positioning in a chondrocyte model [29, 30]. By contrast, an IL-6–STAT3 feedback loop promoted EMT-associated changes and CSC expansion in human breast cancer cells with acquired resistance to PI3K inhibitors, but whether these effects require primary cilia remains unclear [74].

The TME therefore provides a useful framework for connecting ciliary signaling with cancer cell plasticity, but this connection should be interpreted carefully. Evidence that TME cues regulate cilia is not always the same as evidence that ciliary changes directly cause anoikis resistance or stemness. For this review, the strongest interpretation is that primary cilia may act as one context-dependent site where microenvironmental inputs intersect with signaling pathways involved in adhesion remodeling, survival after detachment, and stem-like states. Direct experimental links between TME-regulated ciliary changes and anoikis resistance remain limited and require further validation.

Therapeutic implications
Therapeutic strategies involving primary cilia or cilia-associated pathways remain at an early stage, but they provide a useful way to think about tumor plasticity, survival after detachment, and stem-like states. Because primary cilia can organize selected signaling pathways, changes in ciliary structure or signaling may influence how tumor cells respond to stress and treatment. A recent study of human triple-negative breast cancer biopsies and patient-derived organoids identified late-hybrid, ciliated stem-like cells as a chemoresistant population. Genetic ablation or pharmacological inhibition of primary ciliogenesis suppressed this resistance, providing a state-specific example of therapeutic ciliary dependency [59]. However, this therapeutic concept should be approached cautiously. The primary cilium is not a universal therapeutic target, and not every factor discussed in this section is primary cilium-specific. Some targets are better understood as part of broader cytoskeletal, centrosomal, chromatin-regulatory, or signaling programs, with ciliary relevance depending on the experimental context and whether ciliary readouts were directly measured.

One group of approaches involves factors related to microtubules, centrosomes, or ciliogenesis. TUBB3 is relevant here because it is a microtubule-related protein and has been linked to anoikis resistance and bone metastasis in prostate cancer [45]. In that study, bone-targeted lipid nanoparticles delivering siTUBB3 suppressed anoikis resistance and metastatic progression in vivo [45]. This finding supports the therapeutic relevance of TUBB3 in a defined tumor context, but it should not be interpreted as evidence that TUBB3 is a primary cilium-specific target. PLK4 provides another example. Because PLK4 is linked to centriole biology and centrosome homeostasis, it is relevant to cilia-associated biology but should not be treated as a primary cilium-specific target. PLK4 has also been reported to promote anoikis resistance in p53-deficient mammary epithelial cells [75]. In triple-negative breast cancer, PLK4 inhibition with CFI-400,945 has been explored as a radiosensitizing strategy [76]. These observations are therapeutically relevant, but PLK4 targeting also affects centrosome homeostasis, chromosome segregation, and cell-cycle progression, so ciliary effects need to be evaluated directly.

Pathway-directed strategies are most clearly connected to ciliary biology in the case of Hh signaling. SMO inhibitors such as vismodegib and sonidegib are established treatments for advanced basal cell carcinoma, a tumor type with strong Hh pathway dependence [6, 77–79]. However, resistance and limited efficacy in broader cancer contexts have encouraged attention to downstream GLI inhibition and combination strategies [6, 80]. Wnt-related approaches are also relevant because Wnt signaling can influence cancer stemness, plasticity, and therapy resistance [38, 65]. Strategies targeting different components of Wnt-related signaling, including Frizzled receptors, receptor tyrosine kinase-like orphan receptor family members, and β-catenin-associated transcriptional programs, have been investigated in different experimental settings [38, 65, 81]. These interventions may affect pathways that intersect with ciliary biology, but they should not automatically be considered cilia-directed therapies.

Unresolved questions and future directions
Metastasis represents an advanced stage of cancer progression that involves epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, anoikis resistance, and stem-like states [13–16, 19, 20, 24, 25, 40]. Because EMP is dynamic, longitudinal or lineage-resolved models should track transitions among epithelial, hybrid, and mesenchymal states together with ciliary abundance and signaling output, rather than infer EMP–cilium relationships from static endpoint markers alone [14, 17, 18, 23, 59]. Translating these molecular insights into clinical utility demands more representative experimental systems that can reflect dynamic changes in disseminating tumor cells. Yet, a critical translational gap persists. The field currently struggles to engineer models that can fully capture the dynamic changes of these biological states, rendering the precise quantification of metastatic events—and the screening of drugs to stop them—a persistent bottleneck in oncological research.

Two-dimensional culture is widely used in cancer research but does not fully reproduce the spatial and microenvironmental complexity of tumors. Although experimentally convenient, it lacks the three-dimensional architecture, cell–cell interactions, extracellular matrix context, and oxygen gradients present in native tumors. Three-dimensional (3D) configurations, such as spheroids and organoids, represent a structural restoration, reintroducing critical variables like intercellular tension, ECM stiffness, and oxygen gradients. Yet, these self-organizing models often suffer from stochastic variability, making standardization a persistent hurdle. To bridge the gap between biological complexity and experimental control, the field is advancing toward engineered micro-physiologies—specifically microfluidic chips and bioprinted scaffolds—that allow for the precise, reproducible reconstruction of the metastatic niche [82–84].

The assessment of metastatic capability ultimately requires models that reflect the living organism. Xenograft models are widely used to evaluate metastatic capacity in vivo, but conventional systems provide a limited immune context [85]. The use of immunocompromised hosts can limit assessment of the crosstalk between tumors and the immune surveillance system. Moreover, interspecies metabolic dissonance frequently distorts pharmacokinetic profiles, leading to clinical failures. To bridge this translational gap, the next generation of models employs ‘Humanized’ Chimeras. By grafting human hematopoietic components into the murine host, these models reconstruct a functional immune environment, allowing for the evaluation of therapeutics in a system that more closely approximates the human patient [85].

The primary cilium ultimately emerges not as a static target, but as a context-dependent modulator of oncogenesis. Its influence is defined by a context-dependent pattern: cilia-associated Hh signaling can be therapeutically relevant in basal cell carcinoma, whereas ciliary loss or disruption has been associated with more aggressive behavior in selected tumor models [6, 8, 36, 77, 86, 87]. This context-dependent variability indicates that a uniform therapeutic approach is unlikely to be appropriate. The future of ciliary therapeutics, therefore, demands a more stratified approach—one that rigorously stratifies patients based on the specific ciliary dependency of their tumor. Such stratification may help identify settings in which cilia-associated pathways can be targeted without overlooking contexts where ciliary loss or disruption could have different effects.

Conclusion
Primary cilia provide a context-dependent signaling compartment in which selected extracellular cues and intracellular pathways can be organized. In cancer, their role is not uniform. The strongest mechanistic evidence concerns Hh signaling, where ciliary trafficking and GLI processing are closely linked to pathway activity. Beyond the well-established ciliary requirement of canonical Hh signaling, evidence for ciliary involvement remains pathway- and model-dependent. Within this evidence hierarchy, mammary epithelial and breast cancer studies currently provide the clearest direct connection between EMP and ciliary biology. Defined EMT-associated states can promote primary ciliogenesis and engage Hh–GLI signaling or cilium-dependent GLIS2 regulation, while recent human triple-negative breast cancer data extend this relationship to chemoresistant late-hybrid stem-like cells [57–59]. Primary cilia can spatially coordinate PDGF-AA–PDGFRα, IGF-1–IGF1R, and TGF-β receptor signaling in defined nonmalignant cell systems [11, 12, 31], whereas Wnt/β-catenin and Notch show more variable relationships with ciliary biology [7–10]. PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK are better regarded as downstream or intersecting modules rather than primary cilium-specific pathways. Whether these receptor-associated ciliary mechanisms directly regulate EMP, cancer stemness, or anoikis resistance in tumors remains unresolved.

Future studies should define when primary cilia constrain tumor progression, when they support malignant signaling, and when cilia-associated pathways can be targeted therapeutically. This will require models that measure ciliary status together with epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, anchorage-independent survival, stem-like states, and tumor microenvironmental cues. Therapeutic interpretation should also remain cautious, because several targets discussed in this review, including TUBB3 and PLK4, affect broader cytoskeletal, centrosomal, or cell-cycle programs and are not primary cilium-specific. A clearer distinction between established cilia-dependent mechanisms, tumor-specific findings, and emerging hypotheses will be essential for translating cilia-associated biology into more precise cancer research and treatment strategies [7–8, 20, 45, 75, 76].

paper.title: Spatially resolved transcriptomics identifies epithelial-specific oncogenic signaling networks in ameloblastoma.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND/PURPOSE: Ameloblastoma is a benign odontogenic tumor characterized by locally aggressive growth and a high recurrence rate. Although recurrent mutations such as BRAF V600E have been identified, the epithelial-specific molecular mechanisms underlying tumor initiation and invasion remain incompletely defined. Previous transcriptomic studies have been limited by stromal contamination and lack of spatial resolution.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: An integrative transcriptomic strategy was applied, combining bulk RNA sequencing of fresh ameloblastoma and dental follicular tissues, RNA sequencing of primary cultured ameloblastoma epithelial cells and dental follicular epithelial cells, and spatial transcriptomic profiling of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded ameloblastoma specimens.

RESULTS: Differential expression and functional enrichment analyses identified 871 upregulated and 1464 downregulated genes in tumor tissues, and 360 upregulated and 306 downregulated genes in primary epithelial cells. Integration of these datasets defined a high-confidence set of 75 consistently dysregulated epithelial genes, including BEX1, NOS1, and IRS2, which were validated by quantitative RT-PCR. Pathway enrichment analyses revealed coordinated activation of Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT, MAPK, and Hedgehog signaling pathways. Spatial transcriptomic analysis further demonstrated that BEX1, NOS1, IRS2, Wnt ligands (WNT3A, WNT6, WNT7A), and Hedgehog effectors (GLI1, GLI2) were predominantly upregulated within ameloblastoma tumor epithelial compartments, confirming pathway activation in situ and minimizing stromal confounding.

CONCLUSION: Together, these findings provide a refined molecular characterization of ameloblastoma and demonstrate spatially localized activation of multiple oncogenic signaling pathways within tumor epithelium, extending current single-pathway models of ameloblastoma pathogenesis and supporting the potential development of pathway-based or combinatorial therapeutic strategies.
paper.full_text:
Introduction
Ameloblastoma is a histologically benign yet locally aggressive odontogenic neoplasm arising in the jaws. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification of tumors, ameloblastomas are categorized into three clinicopathological subtypes: solid/multicystic, extraosseous (peripheral), and unicystic forms.1 Despite their benign histological appearance, ameloblastomas are characterized by a high propensity for local recurrence, particularly following conservative surgical management. Consequently, wide surgical excision with adequate margins remains the current standard of care.1

Ameloblastoma is widely regarded as originating from odontogenic epithelium, including the epithelial rests of the dental lamina, the developing enamel organ, epithelial rests of Malassez, the lining epithelium of intrabony odontogenic cysts, and, in peripheral cases, the basal cells of the oral mucosa. Among these proposed progenitor cell populations, the epithelial rests of the dental lamina are considered the most likely cell of origin for ameloblastoma. 1 Tooth development, termed odontogenesis, proceeds through a series of well-defined stages, including the bud, cap, and bell stages. During the cap stage, the apical portion of the proliferating dental lamina expands and invaginates to form the enamel organ, which subsequently interacts with the underlying dental papilla to produce enamel during the bell stage. Following tooth bud formation, the residual dental lamina progressively degenerates into epithelial rests dispersed within the fibrous connective tissue of the dental follicle and the marrow spaces of the jaws. Based on this developmental context, it is widely accepted that genetic aberrations arising within the epithelial rests of the dental lamina may represent an early event contributing to the initiation and subsequent development of ameloblastoma.

Currently, the oncogenic BRAF V600E mutation has been identified as the most prevalent genetic alteration in ameloblastoma, with a reported prevalence of up to 87.2% in study cohorts,2–6 representing the most common genetic alteration and underpin constitutive ERK signaling that promotes epithelial proliferation and survival. Additional evidence implicates Wnt/β-catenin,6–9 PI3K/AKT,10,11 and FGFR12–15 signaling in tumor growth, invasion, and resistance to apoptosis, collectively supporting the concept that ameloblastoma arises from aberrant reactivation of odontogenic epithelial programs. However, despite these insights, the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma remains incompletely defined. Most existing transcriptomic analyses rely on bulk tumor tissues, which are intrinsically confounded by stromal, inflammatory, and vascular components, limiting the ability to resolve tumor epithelial–specific molecular events. Moreover, few studies integrate in vivo tumor profiles with purified odontogenic epithelial cell models or validate gene expression within spatial tissue context, resulting in uncertainty regarding the biological relevance and cellular localization of candidate pathways and genes. Consequently, the precise driver genes that link canonical pathway activation to the locally invasive behavior of ameloblastoma and the molecular heterogeneity beyond well-characterized driver mutations remain insufficiently characterized.

In this study, we sought to elucidate the key epithelial drivers and signaling pathways underlying the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma by integrating complementary transcriptomic approaches. We first performed comparative transcriptome analysis between fresh ameloblastoma tissues and dental follicle tissues, representing the presumed odontogenic origin. To further minimize stromal confounding and enrich for tumor epithelial–specific molecular signatures, we next compared gene expression profiles between primary cultured ameloblastoma epithelial cells and cultured dental epithelial cells derived from dental follicles. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified from these in vivo and in vitro comparisons were subsequently overlapped to define a high-confidence gene set consistently dysregulated in ameloblastoma epithelium. Collectively, this integrative strategy aimed to provide a more refined and biologically relevant understanding of the molecular mechanisms driving ameloblastoma development and local invasiveness.

Clinical samples
Four multicystic ameloblastoma specimens and three dental follicular tissue samples containing abundant odontogenic epithelial rests were obtained from patients undergoing surgical treatment at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, National Taiwan University Hospital, Taiwan. All specimens were collected immediately after surgical excision and processed for downstream analyses. Demographic characteristics, anatomical sites, histopathological subtypes, and BRAF mutation status of all collected samples are summarized in Table 1. This study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of NTUH (No. 201412058RINA, 201608088RINA, and 201901034RIND).

Cell culture
Primary odontogenic epithelial cells derived from dental follicular tissues and primary ameloblastoma epithelial cells were established from freshly resected ameloblastoma specimens through the explant culture method. Briefly, tissues were processed immediately after surgical excision, and the minced tissue were cultured under defined conditions. The cells were maintained in medium composed of CnT-Prime (CnT-PR, Cellntec Advanced cell systems, Bern, Switzerland) and DMEM+10% FBS in 1:1 ratio with adding 1% pen/strip, 5 μM Rock inhibitor (Y-27632) (Cat. No. 1254; Tocris Bioscience, Bristol, UK), 1 μM BMP inhibitor (DMH-1) (Cat. 4126), and 1 μM TGF-β inhibitor (Cat. 2939) in a humidified incubator at 37 °C with 5% CO2. All experiments were performed using early-passage cells to minimize culture-induced phenotypic drift. The demographic and clinicopathological characteristics of samples used for primary cell culture are summarized in Table 1.

Immunohistochemical analysis (IHC)
Cultured epithelial cells derived from dental follicular tissues and ameloblastomas were cultured in chamber slides. After removal of the supernatant, the cells were fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin. Immunohistochemical analysis was performed. Briefly, cells were incubated with primary antibodies, Cytokeratin 19 (Clone RCK108; Agilent/ Dako, Santa Clara, CA, USA) and PITX2 (Clone AF2330; R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA), followed by detection using an appropriate secondary antibody system and chromogenic visualization. Cells were counterstained with hematoxylin. Details of the primary antibodies, antigen retrieval conditions, and detection systems are provided by the respective manufacturers.

RNA isolation
Total RNA was extracted from ameloblastoma and dental follicle fresh tissues and primary cultured epithelial cells from ameloblastomas and dental follicles using TRIzol™ Plus RNA Purification Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA concentration and quality was quantified by nucleic acid concentrations using a Nanodrop Lite spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Only RNA samples meeting quality requirements were used for subsequent analyses.

RNA library preparation and next generation sequencing
RNA sequencing libraries were prepared using the TruSeq Stranded mRNA Sample Preparation Kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, 1 μg of total RNA was used as input, and poly-adenylated mRNA was purified using oligo(dT)-coupled magnetic beads, followed by fragmentation at elevated temperature. First-strand cDNA synthesis was performed using reverse transcriptase and random primers, followed by second-strand cDNA synthesis to generate double-stranded cDNA. After end repair and adenylation of the 3′ends, sequencing adapters were ligated, and the libraries were purified using the AMPure XP system (Beckman Coulter, Beverly, MA, USA). Library quality and fragment size distribution were assessed using an Agilent 2100 Bio-analyzer (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA), and library quantification was performed using a real-time PCR–based method. Qualified libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 500 platform (Illumina) to generate 150-bp paired-end reads. Sequencing was performed by Genomics, BioSci & Tech Co. (New Taipei City, Taiwan).

Transcriptome analysis and identification of differentially expressed genes (DEGs)
Raw sequencing reads were processed and pseudoaligned to the human reference transcriptome (hg38) using the Kallisto algorithm.16 Transcript-level abundance estimates were imported and summarized at the gene level for downstream analysis. Differential gene expression analysis was performed using the DESeq2 package in R.17 Genes were considered differentially expressed if they met the following criteria: an absolute log2 fold change (|log2FC|) greater than 1 and an adjusted P-value <0.05. More stringent thresholds were applied as indicated in specific analyses and figure legends.

Function annotation of DEGs
Functional enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was performed using the Metascape platform (https://metascape.org).18,19 Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis was conducted to evaluate the biological functions of DEGs across three ontology categories: biological processes, cellular components, and molecular functions. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis was carried out to identify significantly enriched signaling pathways associated with the DEGs.20 KEGG analyses were performed using both Metascape and KEGG Mapper (https://www.genome.jp/kegg/). For enrichment analysis, a minimum gene overlap of three was required, and terms with an adjusted P-value <0.05 were considered statistically significant. The enrichment results were visualized using SRplot.21

Reverse transcription (RT) and real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR)
Reverse transcription was performed using Applied Bio-systems™ High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). qRT-PCR was performed using TaqMan Real-Time PCR Assays (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in The CFX Connect Real-Time PCR machine (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA). The primer/probe sets used for this study listed in Additional file 1(https://jds.ads.org.tw/cgi/editor.cgi?article=3487&window=additional_files&context=journal). β-actin was used as the internal reference gene for normalization. Relative gene expression levels were calculated using the 2−ΔΔCt method using dental follicle as control. All experiments were performed in duplicate.

Spatial gene expression analysis
Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue sections were cut at a thickness of 5 μm and mounted onto Visium CytAssist-compatible slides (10x Genomics, Pleasanton, CA, USA). H&E staining was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol, and stained sections were imaged at 20 × magnification using a VS200 slide scanner (Evident Corp., Tokyo, Japan). Spatial transcriptomic analysis was performed using the Visium CytAssist Spatial Gene Expression assay for FFPE tissue (10x Genomics) with the Human Whole Transcriptome Probe Set. Briefly, probes were hybridized to RNA molecules in the tissue sections, followed by ligation and transfer of the probe-derived products onto the Visium slide containing spatially barcoded capture oligonucleotides using the CytAssist instrument (10x Genomics). The resulting ligation products were enzymatically amplified and converted into sequencing-ready libraries according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq X Plus platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). Sequencing reads were aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38) using Space Ranger v3.0.1 (10x Genomics). Spatial gene expression data were visualized and analyzed using Loupe Browser version 8.0.0.

Statistical analysis
Quantitative real-time PCR data were analyzed and visualized using GraphPad Prism 9 software (GraphPad Software Inc., San Diego, CA, USA). Statistical comparisons between groups were performed using either Student’s t-test or Welch’s t-test, as appropriate. A P-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Identification of DEGs and functional analysis between fresh ameloblastoma tumor tissue and dental follicular tissue
To define the molecular landscape of ameloblastoma, tumor tissues from four patients with multicystic ameloblastoma and dental follicular tissues from three patients were subjected to RNA sequencing. As shown in Fig. 1A, principal component analysis (PCA) showed that ameloblastoma and dental follicular tissues segregated in the PC1–PC2 space, with PC1 explaining 39% of the variance and PC2 accounting for an additional 30%. Differential expression analysis identified 871 upregulated and 1464 downregulated genes in ameloblastoma compared with dental follicular tissues (|log2FC| > 1, adjusted P < 0.01; Fig. 1B) (detailed information is provided in Additional file 2(https://jds.ads.org.tw/cgi/editor.cgi?article=3487&window=additional_files&context=journal)). GO enrichment analysis revealed that upregulated genes were predominantly associated with ribosome- and translation-related cellular components (e.g., cytosolic ribosome), whereas downregulated genes were enriched in immune- and inflammation-related biological processes (Fig. 1C). KEGG pathway analysis revealed that the significantly upregulated genes in ameloblastoma were enriched in pathways related to Wnt and Hippo signaling, hormone signaling, and transcriptional misregulation, whereas downregulated genes were associated with cell adhesion molecules, chemokine signaling, PI3K–AKT signaling, and other immune- and cytoskeleton-related pathways (Fig. 1D), the majority of which have been implicated in dysregulation of cell proliferation, cell cycle, differentiation, and migration.

Identification of DEGs and functional analysis between ameloblastoma epithelial cells and dental follicular epithelial cells
To verify the DEGs identified from tissue samples and minimize potential stromal and inflammatory influences, primary epithelial cells were cultured separately from two ameloblastoma and three dental follicular specimens, and their odontogenic epithelial nature was validated by positive immunostaining for odontogenic epithelial markers CK19 and PITX2 (Fig. 2).22,23 PCA revealed that dental follicular cells clustered closely and were clearly separated from ameloblastoma cells, indicating preservation of their original phenotypic characteristics during in vitro culture (Fig. 3A). Differential expression analysis identified 360 upregulated and 306 downregulated genes in ameloblastoma cells compared with dental follicular cells (|log2FC| > 1, adjusted P < 0.01; Fig. 3B; Additional file 3(https://jds.ads.org.tw/cgi/editor.cgi?article=3487&window=additional_files&context=journal)). GO analysis revealed that upregulated genes were predominantly associated with extracellular matrix components and organization (including extracellular matrix and basement membrane), tissue and skin development, connective tissue morphogenesis, and epithelial–mesenchymal transition, whereas downregulated genes were mainly enriched in immune- and defense-related biological processes, including inflammatory response, and the regulation of immune and cytokine-mediated signaling pathways (Fig. 3C). KEGG analysis showed enrichment of the Wnt signaling pathway among upregulated genes—consistent with findings from tissue samples—along with immune and metabolic pathways among downregulated genes (Fig. 3D).

Overlap analysis revealed shared DEGs in ameloblastoma tissues and primary cultured ameloblastoma cells
Since our goal was to identify the key pathways involved the genesis of ameloblastoma, overlap analysis was performed between the 871 and 360 upregulated genes, and between the 1464 and 306 downregulated genes, identified in tissue samples and primary cultured epithelial cells, respectively. We found 26 and 49 genes that were commonly upregulated and downregulated, respectively, in both tissue samples and primary cultured epithelial cells (Fig. 4; Table 2). Of these 75 DEGs, genes associated with signaling pathways implicated in the pathogenesis of odontogenic lesions, including the PI3K/AKT, MAPK, Hedgehog, and Wnt pathways,24,25 were selected for validation by RT-qPCR. Accordingly, the expression levels of brain-expressed X-linked protein 1 (BEX1), nitric oxide synthase 1 (NOS1), and insulin receptor substrate 2 (IRS2) were examined and found to be upregulated in ameloblastoma tissues compared with dental follicle tissues, with IRS2 showing a statistically significant increase (Fig. 5).

Whole transcriptome spatial in situ data validate selected DEGs, activators of Wnt/β-catenin and hedgehog signaling pathways in ameloblastoma tissue
To further characterize the spatial organization of tumor and stromal components and to localize pathway-related gene expression within ameloblastoma tissues, spatial transcriptomic analysis was performed. Histopathological annotation, gene expression–based clustering, and dimensionality reduction were integrated to delineate distinct cellular compartments and signaling activities within the tumor microenvironment. As shown in Fig. 6A and B, gene expression–based clustering showed high concordance with the oral pathologist’s histopathological annotations. Dimensionality reduction using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) further resolved distinct cellular compartments, including peripheral and central tumor epithelial cells, tumor-associated stroma, subepithelial fibrous tissue, and squamous epithelium (Fig. 6C). Spatial expression mapping demonstrated that the selected DEGs, including IRS2, BEX1, and NOS1, were upregulated in ameloblastoma tumor regions (Fig. 6D). Consistent with pathway enrichment analyses, activators of the Wnt signaling pathway, including T cell factor 7 (TCF7), WNT3A, WNT6, and WNT7A, were also predominantly upregulated in ameloblastoma tumor cells (Fig. 6E). Additionally, the Hedgehog pathway transcriptional effectors GLI family zinc finger 1 (GLI1) and GLI2 were preferentially upregulated in ameloblastoma tumor epithelial compartments (Fig. 6F). Taken together, these spatial transcriptomic findings corroborate the differential expression and pathway enrichment results obtained from bulk tissue and primary cell analyses, highlighting the spatially localized activation of oncogenic signaling pathways within ameloblastoma tumor epithelium.

Discussion
Ameloblastoma is the most common odontogenic neoplasm of jaws with unknown pathogenesis and is characterized by locally aggressive behavior and a high recurrence rate, despite being histologically benign. Currently, surgical excision with adequate margins remains the standard treatment,1 extensive excision often leads to significant functional and esthetic morbidity. The identification of BRAF V600E mutation in ameloblastoma has enabled the use of MAPK pathway inhibitors in selected unresectable cases.26,27 However, only approximately 60–80% of ameloblastoma harbor this mutation, and residual tumors are often still identified after BRAF/ERK-targeted therapy, likely because MAPK pathway inhibition alone is insufficient to achieve complete tumor eradication, underscoring the need to further elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying ameloblastoma pathogenesis.28,29

In this study, we integrated bulk tissue RNA sequencing, primary epithelial cell transcriptomics, and spatial transcriptomic profiling to delineate the molecular alterations underlying ameloblastoma. DEG analyses from both fresh tissues and cultured epithelial cells identified upregulation of BEX1, NOS1, and IRS2. Mechanistically, BEX1 has been reported to inhibit the Wnt/β-catenin pathway suppressor RUNX3,30,31 thereby indirectly enhancing β-catenin activity. NOS1 promotes S-nitrosylation–mediated degradation of PTEN,32,33 a key negative regulator of PI3K/AKT signaling, which also facilitates nuclear accumulation of β-catenin. 34,35 IRS2 functions as a central adaptor linking receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) activation to downstream PI3K/AKT and MAPK signaling through PI3K activation and growth factor receptor-bound protein 2 (GRB2) phosphorylation. 36–39 Importantly, the upregulation of these DEGs was consistent with spatial transcriptomic analysis, which mitigates potential confounding effects from stromal and inflammatory components to further support that these genes were predominantly upregulated in tumor epithelial compartments, thereby providing in situ validation of their tumor-specific expression patterns.

Given that these DEGs converge on signaling networks, particularly Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT, and MAPK pathways, it is likely that coordinated pathway dysregulation rather than isolated signaling events in ameloblastoma. Indeed, activation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway plays a central role in multiple tumor-related biological processes, including tumorigenesis, proliferation, differentiation, invasion, and tissue homeostasis. Canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling is characterized by stabilization and nuclear translocation of β-catenin, resulting in transcriptional activation of downstream target genes essential for early odontogenesis.40–43 In fact, aberrant β-catenin expression has been reported in ameloblastoma and other odontogenic carcinomas.8,44–46 Notably, mutations in exon 3 of catenin beta 1 (CTNNB1), which encodes β-catenin, have been identified in approximately 50% of adenoid variant ameloblastomas, with more than 90% of CTNNB1-mutant tumors exhibiting nuclear β-catenin immunoreactivity;42,47 importantly, these CTNNB1-mutant ameloblastomas often lack concurrent BRAF or KRAS mutations,42,47 indicating activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling through a MAPK-independent mechanism. In the present study, spatial transcriptomic analysis revealed overexpression of multiple Wnt pathway activators in ameloblastoma tumor cells. Collectively, these findings further substantiate a contributory role of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the pathogenesis of a subset of ameloblastomas.

In addition to Wnt/β-catenin and MAPK signaling, our spatial transcriptomic analysis also indicated activation of the Hedgehog pathway in ameloblastoma, as evidenced by elevated expression of its transcriptional effectors GLI1 and GLI2. Hedgehog signaling plays a critical role in cell growth and differentiation and is aberrantly activated in several malignancies, including medulloblastoma, basal cell carcinoma, and glioblastoma.8,48–50 Previous studies have reported activating mutations in SMO in a subset of ameloblastomas.4 As a key upstream regulator of Hedgehog signaling, activating SMO mutations lead to increased GLI1 expression and sustained pathway activation, providing a plausible mechanism for the elevated GLI1 and GLI2 expression observed in this study. Even in the absence of smoothened (SMO) mutation, GLI1 overexpression has been identified in subsets of ameloblastoma, supporting the role of Hedgehog pathway activation in tumorigenesis.51 Taken together, these findings indicate that ameloblastoma is characterized by coordinated dysregulation of multiple oncogenic signaling pathways, including Wnt/β-catenin, MAPK, PI3K/AKT, and Hedgehog signaling, which collectively contribute to tumor initiation and progression.

While our study provides integrative transcriptomic insights into the molecular alterations underlying ameloblastoma, a limitation of this study is the use of dental follicular tissue as the control for ameloblastoma. Although dental follicle is commonly adopted in odontogenic tumor studies, the most biologically appropriate controls would be developing tooth germs with normal odontogenic epithelial cells, which more closely represent the putative cell of origin of ameloblastoma. However, these tissues are exceedingly difficult to obtain in sufficient quantity and purity for transcriptomic analyses, particularly in human samples, necessitating the use of dental follicular tissue as a practical and ethically feasible alternative.

In conclusion, this study integrated bulk tissue transcriptomics, primary epithelial cell analyses, and spatial transcriptomic profiling to provide a comprehensive molecular characterization of ameloblastoma. Our findings identified a set of reproducibly dysregulated genes and revealed coordinated perturbation of multiple oncogenic signaling pathways, including Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT, MAPK, and Hedgehog signaling, with spatially localized activation within tumor epithelial compartments. These results highlighted the molecular heterogeneity and network-level dysregulation underlying ameloblastoma pathogenesis and extended current understanding beyond single-pathway models. Collectively, this integrative framework may facilitate more refined molecular classification of ameloblastoma and inform future studies aim at developing pathway-based or combinatorial therapeutic strategies.

paper.title: Structure-based discovery of potent SMO inhibitors guided by MM/GBSA binding free energies in hedgehog-driven cancers.
paper.abstract: The Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway, crucial for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis, is frequently dysregulated in cancers, making its core component, the Smoothened (SMO) receptor, a prime therapeutic target. This study employed an integrative computational strategy to identify novel SMO inhibitors. Virtual screening of the ZINC database highlighted ZINC000299767263 (ZINC7263) as a top candidate, exhibiting a Glide score of -10.86 and MM/GBSA binding energy of -65.3 kJ/mol, comparable to the FDA-approved inhibitor Vismodegib. Molecular docking revealed critical interactions with SMO residues Asp384, Arg400, and Gln477, supported by hydrophobic contacts with Phe484 and Trp480. Molecular dynamics simulations (200 ns) demonstrated stable binding, with root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) and fluctuation (RMSF) analyses confirming complex stability. Free energy decomposition underscored contributions from Asp384, Arg400, and Gln477, aligning with Vismodegib's binding mechanism. ZINC7263 adhered to drug-likeness criteria (Lipinski's rule of five, Jorgensen's rule of three) and exhibited favorable pharmacokinetics, including high oral absorption (89.45%) and blood-brain barrier permeability (logBB = -1.01). Induced-fit docking further validated its binding mode, highlighting a conserved interaction profile. These findings position ZINC7263 as a novel, potent SMO inhibitor with a stable binding affinity, dynamic interaction stability, and promising preclinical potential for targeting Hh-driven cancers. Its unique scaffold and optimized pharmacokinetic profile advocate for advanced in vitro and in vivo studies to translate these computational insights into therapeutic applications.

paper.title: SHH mediated human dopaminergic neuron differentiation is facilitated by transcription factor ZIC3.
paper.journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular cell research
paper.abstract: Distinct neuronal subtype specification involves a complex network of transcription factors (TF). Previous studies from our laboratory showed Zinc finger transcription factor of cerebellum (ZIC) 3 to regulate the expression of Tyrosine Hydroxylase (TH), a proxy marker for dopaminergic (DA) neurons, in mouse olfactory bulb (OB) and mid brain (MB) neurons by distinct mechanisms. In absence of ZIC3 consensus binding site in proximal region of mouse TH promoter, ZIC3 interacts with ER81 in OB and regulates TH expression whereas in absence of ER81 in midbrain, ZIC3 regulates TH by enhancing the expression of PITX3. To analyze whether this observation is evolutionarily conserved in humans, different human stem cell model systems were utilized to understand the role of ZIC3 in human DA generation. Differentiation of dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs) with proper cues resulted in the expression of TH. Gain and loss of function demonstrated ZIC3 to be essential for the expression of TH. ZIC3 activates the transcription of TH gene by binding to response element within the region of TH promoter. Addition of SHH, a known morphogen that facilitates dopaminergic differentiation, increased the expression of TH, however, this regulation was suppressed in the absence of ZIC3. Mechanistic insight demonstrated SHH influences ZIC3 expression by GLI protein binding to ZIC3 promoter. Similar role of ZIC3 in TH expression was observed in hiPSCs differentiated to DA like neurons. Conclusively, the present study for the first time demonstrates the undetermined importance of ZIC3 in SHH mediated TH specification in cells of human origin.

paper.title: Immunohistochemical evaluation of Ki-67 and GLI1 in sporadic and nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome-associated odontogenic keratocysts.
paper.journal: Revista espanola de patologia : publicacion oficial de la Sociedad Espanola de Anatomia Patologica y de la Sociedad Espanola de Citologia
paper.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) is a developmental odontogenic cyst that may occur sporadically (OKCsp) or in association with nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (NBCCS) (OKC-sy). NBCCS is an autosomal dominant disorder characterised by morphological abnormalities and an increased predisposition to several neoplasms, including basal cell carcinomas. Mutations in the tumour suppressor gene PTCH1 have been reported in patients with OKC and NBCCS. PTCH1 participates in a signalling cascade that culminates in the translocation of GLI transcription factors to the nucleus, thereby activating target genes involved in cell proliferation. Aberrant GLI1 expression has been associated with increased proliferation in lung adenocarcinoma and other cancers.

OBJECTIVE: To compare GLI1 and Ki-67 protein expression in OKCs associated with NBCCS versus sporadic OKCs.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: We included 13 OKCsp and 9 OKCsy from a children's hospital and university ... Immunohistochemistry was performed using anti-GLI1 and anti-Ki-67 to assess GLI1 expression and cell proliferation.

RESULTS: No significant differences were observed in GLI1 or Ki-67 expression in the epithelial component of OKCsy versus OKCsp. A positive correlation between GLI1 and Ki-67 expression was detected in the total sample (r = 0.71, p < 0.05).

CONCLUSION: The positive correlation between GLI1 and Ki-67 expression in OKCs suggests an association between SHH pathway activity and cell proliferation in both sporadic and syndromic lesions.

paper.title: Short-term low-protein feeding accelerated skin wound healing by promoting re-epithelialization, inflammation resolution, granulation tissue formation and remodeling in largemouth bass, Micropterus salmoides.
paper.abstract: The present study evaluated the effect of short-term feeding with graded dietary protein levels on skin wound healing in largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides). Three isolipidic diets containing 48% (P48), 52% (P52), and 56% (P56) crude protein were fed to fish (initial mean weight 13.00 g) for 5 weeks, followed by a standardized mechanical skin-wounding challenge. Wound repair was assessed at 1, 3, and 7 days post-wounding (dpw). The P52 diet supported better growth performance than the P48 diet. However, P48 accelerated wound closure and promoted more advanced histological repair, characterized by earlier re-epithelialization, more efficient necrotic tissue clearance, reduced wound bed area, and a thinner, more mature neo-epidermis. At the molecular level, P48 induced early upregulation of re-epithelialization-related genes, including mmp2, mmp9, and egf, accompanied by stronger MMP9 immunohistochemical signals. P48 was also associated with rapid inflammatory activation, shown by early increases in MPO, NAG, and LZM activities and il1b and tnfa expression, followed by faster inflammatory resolution and sustained il10 upregulation. In addition, P48 showed higher antimicrobial-defense-related markers and stronger extracellular-matrix-, angiogenesis-, and collagen-associated responses, as evidenced by higher expression of hamp, prf, fn1, lamb2, vegf, shh, and col1a1, stronger CD31-positive immunofluorescence signals, and greater collagen fiber accumulation. Western blotting further showed that FN1, SHH, and CCN1 protein responses were broadly consistent with their corresponding transcript-level patterns. Temporal response analysis further indicated a coordinated transition from early epithelial and inflammatory responses to later repair and remodeling responses. Correlation analysis showed that reduced wound area was significantly and negatively associated with both ccn1 transcript abundance and CCN1 protein abundance. These findings indicate that short-term low-protein feeding enhances skin wound healing and may represent a stage-specific nutritional strategy for farmed largemouth bass.

paper.title: Theragenerative Nanomaterials: Integrating Therapy, Regeneration, and Diagnosis-Navigating the Shared Pathways Between Tissue Repair and Malignancy.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nanotechnology convergence with regenerative medicine and oncology creates opportunities and challenges. Nanomaterials can be programmed to modulate biological responses, yet tissue repair and cancer share fundamental signaling pathways-including Wnt/β-catenin, Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase (MAPK)/ Extracellular Signal-Regulated Kinase (ERK), Notch, and Hedgehog-raising a critical concern: pro-regenerative stimuli may inadvertently activate malignant programs. This review introduces the "theragenerative" paradigm, defined as nanomaterial platforms that concurrently integrate therapeutic (anti-cancer), regenerative (tissue repair), and diagnostic (real-time monitoring) functions. We examine the dual role of nanomaterials at the regenerative-oncology interface and propose context-aware platforms that dynamically balance healing and anti-tumor effects while minimizing oncogenic risk. Unlike conventional reviews that separately address nanocarriers for drug delivery or scaffolds for tissue engineering, this review is explicitly organized around the central question of how to establish safe boundaries between regenerative signals and tumor-promoting pathways-a distinction that defines the theragenerative framework.

METHODS: We critically reviewed the literature on nanostructured scaffolds, cell-instructive surfaces, stimuli-responsive nanocarriers (pH, redox, enzyme, hypoxia), and biomimetic cell membrane-coated platforms, synthesizing findings from both foundational and recent studies. Studies on Extracellular Matrix (ECM) mimicry, tumor microenvironment-responsive drug delivery, and theragenerative systems were analyzed. Key shared pathways and translational challenges (safety, scalability, regulation, AI) were assessed.

RESULTS: Nanostructured scaffolds guide stem cell behavior and promote tissue repair by recreating ECM cues. Smart nanocarriers exploiting TME triggers (acidic pH, high glutathione, overexpressed Matrix Metalloproteinase (MMPs)) achieve precise drug delivery with reduced off-target effects. Theragenerative platforms combine therapy, regeneration, and diagnostics for real-time monitoring. However, the shared pathways-particularly Wnt/β-catenin, Notch, Hedgehog, and YAP/TAZ-pose a dual-edged risk: their activation promotes regeneration but may inadvertently drive malignant transformation, while their inhibition suppresses tumors but can impair tissue repair. This necessitates precise, context-dependent nanoparticle programming to navigate this therapeutic dilemma. Major hurdles include long-term genotoxicity, immunogenicity, manufacturing scalability, regulatory pathways for combination products, and AI-driven optimization.

CONCLUSION: Smart nanomaterials that sense their surroundings can operate at the crossroads of regenerative medicine and oncology. They either promote tissue repair or trigger tumor cell death while sparing healthy tissues. Successful clinical adoption requires a system that selectively modulates signaling pathways, restricts activity to defined sites, and controls timing precisely. This strategy could revolutionize personalized treatment for patients who simultaneously suffer from cancer and tissue defects.

Introduction
Biomaterial science has been fundamentally reshaped over the last few decades, transitioning from an era of passive, non-reactive implants to the current age of smart, biologically interactive constructs.1 At first, biomaterials were chosen mainly based on their mechanical performance and biocompatibility, aiming to function as implants that could replace or reinforce damaged tissues with as little negative immune reaction as possible.2 Metals, ceramics, and polymers formed the foundation of early biomedical implants, with success measured largely by their inertness and durability within the host environment.3

The emergence of nanoscale science has significantly reshaped this framework. Operating within the 1–100 nm size range, researchers can now fabricate materials with high precision, offering significant control over both their intrinsic attributes and their performance within biological environments. These nanostructures are distinguished by distinctive physicochemical traits—such as greatly enhanced surface-area-to-mass ratios, quantum confinement phenomena, and optical, magnetic, and catalytic behaviors that vary with size—features that are completely absent in their bulk equivalent.4 Such characteristics have paved the way for new opportunities in medicine, allowing for the design of substances that dynamically engage with physiological pathways, as opposed to functioning solely as inert scaffolds.5 The emergence of responsive nanomaterials has introduced a new generation of biomedical tools that can sense their surroundings and alter their behavior accordingly. Their versatility permits the integration of multiple clinically relevant actions, such as thermal ablation of tumors, regulated drug elution, and visual diagnostics, in parallel with providing the physical framework essential for successful tissue engineering and regeneration.6 This convergence of therapeutic, diagnostic, and regenerative functions within single nanomaterial platforms represents a paradigm shift in biomedical materials science.7

Within this paradigm, we define “theragenerative nanomedicine” as a distinct class of smart nanomaterials designed to concurrently execute three interconnected functions: (1) therapeutic— delivering anti-cancer agents or physical stimuli (eg, photothermal, photodynamic) to eliminate malignant cells; (2) regenerative— providing structural and biochemical cues that guide stem cell behavior and promote tissue repair; and (3) diagnostic— enabling real-time monitoring of treatment response and tissue regeneration via imaging or biosensing modalities. This tripartite functionality distinguishes theragenerative platforms from conventional nanocarriers that primarily focus on a single application, drawing inspiration from the established concepts of theranostics and regenerative biomaterials. The scientific boundary of this paradigm lies in the deliberate integration of pro-regenerative and anti-malignant cues within a single nanomaterial system, with the explicit goal of navigating the therapeutic window where tissue repair and tumor suppression must be simultaneously achieved. The clinical relevance of this framework is particularly evident in scenarios where tissue repair and cancer risk coexist, including: (i) post-tumor resection reconstruction, where scaffolds must prevent local recurrence while promoting healing of surgical defects;8 (ii) bone regeneration in cancer patients, where osteoconductive materials must avoid stimulating residual tumor cells or creating a pro-metastatic niche;9 (iii) radiotherapy- and chemotherapy-induced tissue damage, where nanomaterials must simultaneously protect or regenerate injured normal tissues while not interfering with systemic anti-tumor efficacy;10 and (iv) wound healing in cancer-susceptible individuals, where regenerative stimuli must be carefully calibrated to avoid inadvertent oncogenic activation in genetically predisposed tissues.11

A fundamental insight is that regeneration and cancer exist on a continuum of cellular behavior, orchestrated by evolutionarily conserved pathways – Wnt/β-catenin, MAPK-ERK, Notch, and Hedgehog – that control stem cell fate and tissue patterning.12 Wnt/β-catenin signaling exemplifies this duality: it governs stem cell renewal and tissue homeostasis, yet its dysregulation is linked to developmental disorders, degenerative diseases, and multiple cancers. Recent work has identified a Wnt-NAD+ axis influencing aging and regeneration through shared regulators (sirtuins, Poly (ADP-Ribose) Polymerase (PARPs), metabolic enzymes); Dysregulation affecting either of these signaling cascades has been consistently linked to oncogenesis, aging-related functional deterioration, and compromised tissue healing capabilities.12–14

Importantly, the effects of these shared pathways are not binary but are critically dependent on dose, timing, cell type, and mutation background.
