While ligand modification can significantly enhance cellular uptake in receptor-positive cells (yielding 3–10× higher intracellular drug levels in receptor-rich tumors such as Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2+) breast cancer with 106 receptors/cell or Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen (PSMA+) prostate cancer),64 its contribution to overall tumor tissue enrichment is more modest—typically increasing accumulation from 5–10% to 15–25% of injected dose.65 This distinction is often overlooked in the literature, leading to overstated claims about targeting efficacy.66

EPR effect, arising from the distinct pathophysiological characteristics of solid tumors, constitutes the foundational principle upon which passive targeting—and consequently nanocarrier-based anticancer therapy—was originally established. This phenomenon facilitates the selective extravasation of nanoscale delivery systems through the abnormally fenestrated tumor vasculature, coupled with their sustained retention resulting from inadequate lymphatic clearance.67 This approach eliminates reliance on targeting ligands by exploiting finely tuned physicochemical parameters: particle dimensions are confined to the 50–150 nm range—sufficiently small to surpass renal filtration (threshold <10 nm) yet large enough to avoid splenic clearance (above 200 nm); surface charge is maintained near neutrality (zeta potential between −10 and +10 mV) to reduce opsonization and subsequent macrophage recognition; and PEGylation imparts a “stealth” character that extends systemic circulation from a matter of minutes to 12–24 hours.68 The clinical viability of this passive strategy is well-illustrated by PEGylated liposomal Doxil®, which achieves a 16-fold enhancement in tumor drug accumulation relative to free Doxil® (AUC 590 μg·h/mL vs 36 μg·h/mL), leading to improved objective response rates of 20–40% among ovarian cancer patients while concurrently lowering the incidence of hand-foot syndrome from 37% to 9%.69

Nevertheless, the clinical translation of passive targeting is hindered by substantial inter-tumoral and inter-patient variability in its efficacy. In contrast to the highly permeable vasculature characteristic of murine xenografts, human neoplasms frequently exhibit diminished vascular fenestrations, which contributes to inconsistent nanoparticle deposition.67 This heterogeneity has been corroborated by quantitative Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging employing 89Zr-labeled nanocarriers, which demonstrates that well-vascularized peripheral regions accumulate 2–3 times more particles than avascular necrotic zones.70 Compounding this issue are dense stromal matrices, elevated interstitial fluid pressure (ranging from 10–40 mmHg in malignant tissues versus 0–3 mmHg in healthy counterparts), and heterogeneous perfusion patterns, all of which collectively impede nanoparticle transport and culminate in delivery efficiencies that can plummet to a mere 0.7–5% of the administered dose in certain solid malignancies. These obstacles are especially formidable in poorly permeable tumors, such as pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, where desmoplastic reactions severely restrict diffusive transport and interspecies discrepancies in EPR magnitude render clinical predictions difficult.71 Added to this are biological impediments including reticuloendothelial system sequestration—predominantly within the liver and spleen—and densely crosslinked extracellular matrices that constrain particle movement even after extravasation, resulting in preferential drug accumulation at tumor margins rather than in deeper parenchymal regions.72 In response, recent engineering innovations—including protease-activated size-shrinkable nanocarriers that undergo reduction from ~100 nm to <20 nm in enzyme-rich microenvironments, alongside vascular normalization strategies employing agents such as anti-VEGF antibodies—are being developed to enhance both the depth and uniformity of intratumoral penetration.73

Active targeting has emerged from the recognition of passive delivery’s limitations, employing surface-conjugated ligands—antibodies (or scFv fragments), RGD peptides (αvβ3 integrins), aptamers, or folate—to enhance specificity and drive receptor-mediated uptake, yielding 3–10× higher intracellular drug levels in receptor-rich tumors (e.g, HER2+ breast cancer with 106 receptors/cell, PSMA+ prostate cancer).64 Optimal ligand densities (0.5–2% surface area) balance avidity gains (10–100× via multivalency) against immune clearance risks (anti-PEG antibodies can reduce circulation by 50–70%). Trastuzumab-liposomes against HER2 achieve 4× greater SK-BR-3 uptake (IC50 0.1 vs 0.4 μg/mL) and extend xenograft survival from 28 to 42 days.66 Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) studies show active targeting raises tumor accumulation from 5–10% to 15–25% while reducing liver uptake from 40% to 20%; anti- Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) cetuximab-nanoparticles for glioblastoma leverage transferrin receptor shuttling for BBB crossing, delivering 2–3× higher glioma penetration.74

Active targeting faces challenges: antigen heterogeneity (only 60–80% tumors express sufficient target), ligand loss, and endosomal entrapment (pH 5.5–6.0 causes <30% release). Fusogenic pH-sensitive peptides improve cytosolic escape by 50–80%.75 MM-302 (HER2-liposomal Doxil®) showed 11% vs 0% objective response in Phase II breast cancer trials, but Progression-Free Survival (PFS) gains were modest (7.6 vs 5.5 months) due to clearance in PEG-immunized patients.76 Dual RGD/transferrin micelles combine EPR with active uptake to bypass P-gp efflux (intracellular Doxil® 2.5 vs 0.5 μM), yielding 5–7× efficacy in resistant models.77 Future designs use MMP2-cleavable linkers to unmask ligands in TME, reducing peripheral binding and extending half-life 2–3×; orthotopic pancreatic models achieved 90% tumor inhibition vs 50% with static ligands.78 Thus, active targeting refines precision therapy (potentially widening therapeutic windows 5–10×) but requires companion diagnostics for patient stratification.79 This shift from passive to receptor-mediated delivery marks a key nanocarrier evolution, addressing old limitations while enabling personalized cancer therapy.80

pH-Responsive Systems
TME is characterized by an acidic pH, with extracellular values ranging from 6.5 to 7.2—considerably higher than the 4.5–5.5 pH found within endosomal compartments—making it a valuable endogenous trigger for the design of smart nanocarriers.81 pH-responsive delivery systems are engineered to maintain stability during systemic circulation (at physiological pH 7.4) while undergoing structural disassembly or degradation upon exposure to the acidic TME, thereby enabling site-specific drug release.82

A representative illustration of this design philosophy is the VC@Lipo nanocarrier developed by Zhang et al, which encapsulates ultrasmall VOx nanozymes within a liposomal bilayer modified with the photosensitizer chlorin e6 (Ce6). This nanocarrier exhibits a uniform diameter of approximately 35 nm and displays excellent stability under physiological conditions (pH 7.4). However, upon exposure to weakly acidic environments mimicking the TME (pH 6.5), the liposomal structure undergoes degradation, facilitating the controlled release of the VOx nanozyme.83,84 Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirmed this pH-responsive behavior: following 3 hours of incubation at pH 6.5, both VOx and VC@Lipo nanostructures exhibited significant collapse, whereas they remained almost entirely intact at pH 7.4. This degradation was further substantiated by UV–vis absorption spectroscopy—which revealed decreased absorbance—and dynamic light scattering (DLS), which demonstrated increased hydrated particle size under acidic conditions. Notably, the degradation rate was accelerated at 37°C relative to 25°C, indicating faster drug release at physiological temperature.83

Importantly, the released VOx nanozyme displays peroxidase (POD)-like activity that is strongly pH-dependent.85 Using 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) as a chromogenic substrate, Zhang et al demonstrated that VOx efficiently catalyzes the generation of hydroxyl radicals (•OH) at pH 4.5–6.0, with peak activity in weakly acidic environments, whereas negligible activity was observed at pH 7.4.86 This pH-dependent catalytic profile confines the Fenton-like reaction to tumors, minimizing off-target effects. Michaelis–Menten analysis gave a Km of 8.86 mM for H2O2, confirming VOx’s POD-mimetic nature, while electron spin resonance (ESR) (with 5,5-Dimethyl-1-Pyrroline N-Oxide (DMPO)) confirmed •OH generation specifically with H2O2 under acidic conditions.83 The loading efficiencies of VOx and Ce6 within the nanocarrier were determined to be 22.9% and 11.8%, respectively. Based on prior evidence that liposomes within the 10–150 nm size range can accumulate at tumor sites via the EPR effect, the approximately 35 nm diameter of the VC@Lipo nanocarrier facilitates both targeted delivery and tumor accumulation of the nanozyme, while simultaneously mitigating premature metabolic clearance during systemic circulation.82 This pH-responsive design not only enables tumor-specific drug release but also activates catalytic activity precisely within the TME, establishing a robust platform for chemodynamic therapy (CDT).83

It is important to note, however, that mildly acidic pH conditions are not unique to tumors. Inflammatory tissues (e.g, rheumatoid arthritis, infected wounds) and ischemic tissues (e.g, myocardial infarction, stroke) also exhibit extracellular pH values in the 6.5–7.0 range due to increased metabolic activity, hypoxia, and immune cell infiltration.87 Consequently, pH-responsive nanocarriers may release their payload in non-malignant inflammatory or ischemic sites, potentially contributing to off-target effects.88 This limitation underscores the need for multi-stimulus strategies that combine pH responsiveness with tumor-specific signals (e.g, enzyme overexpression, hypoxia) to achieve greater selectivity.81

While pH-responsive nanocarriers enable tumor-selective drug release, several regenerative considerations must be addressed. First, mildly acidic pH (6.5–7.0) is not unique to tumors; inflammatory tissues (rheumatoid arthritis, infected wounds, myocardial infarction, and ischemic tissues) also exhibit acidic microenvironments due to increased metabolic activity, hypoxia, and immune cell infiltration.88 Thus, pH-responsive release may occur in regenerating tissues where inflammation is present, potentially impairing repair by releasing cytotoxic payloads at healing sites.89 Second, acidic pH is characteristic of the early wound healing environment, where immune cells create localized acidosis to facilitate bacterial clearance and matrix remodeling; pH-responsive nanocarriers could inadvertently release drugs that suppress these essential regenerative processes.87 Third, mesenchymal stem cells in the bone marrow niche are sensitive to pH fluctuations; sustained drug release triggered by local acidosis could impair stem cell function, osteogenic differentiation, and hematopoietic stem cell renewal.90 Fourth, pH-responsive scaffolds designed for bone regeneration must consider that osteoclasts create acidic microenvironments (pH ~4.5) during bone resorption, potentially triggering premature drug release that could interfere with the delicate balance between bone formation and resorption.88 These limitations underscore the need for multi-stimulus strategies combining pH responsiveness with tumor-specific signals (e.g, enzyme overexpression, hypoxia, or specific tumor antigens) to achieve greater selectivity and preserve regenerative capacity in non-malignant tissues.81

Redox-Responsive Systems
Redox-responsive nanocarriers are designed to capitalize on the prominent redox differentials that exist between intracellular and extracellular compartments, as well as between neoplastic and normal tissues. Malignant cells are distinguished by markedly elevated glutathione (GSH) concentrations—typically in the range of 2–10 mM intracellularly, compared with only 2–20 μM in the extracellular milieu—which constitute a primary antioxidant defense against reactive oxygen species (ROS). The maintenance of redox equilibrium, achieved through the balanced production and scavenging of ROS, is essential for normal cellular metabolism. GSH, as the principal intracellular antioxidant, plays a central role in regulating this oxidation–reduction balance.36,91,92 When the burden of ROS—including singlet oxygen (1O2), hydroxyl radicals (•OH), and superoxide anions (O2•−)—exceeds the cellular antioxidant capacity, oxidative stress ensues and ultimately leads to cell death.81 To avert ROS-mediated damage, cancer cells have evolved a self-regulatory mechanism that upregulates endogenous GSH levels to neutralize these reactive species. By mitigating oxidative stress, this adaptive response not only supports tumor proliferation but also markedly compromises the efficacy of ROS-based therapeutic modalities, including CDT, photodynamic therapy (PDT), and sonodynamic therapy (SDT).93

Strategies that simultaneously generate ROS and deplete GSH offer a powerful approach to amplify oxidative stress and enhance therapeutic efficacy.61 The VC@Lipo nanocarrier system embodies this dual-action redox-responsive strategy. It is important to note, however, that this platform has been validated exclusively in 4T1 breast cancer cells in vitro and has not yet been evaluated in tissue regeneration models, let alone in combined cancer-associated repair settings. Following pH-triggered degradation, the mixed-valence VOx nanozyme decomposes into V4+ and V5+ species.83 While V4+ participates in Fenton-like reactions to generate toxic •OH, V5+ actively depletes intracellular GSH through redox reactions. This GSH consumption capability was quantitatively evaluated using 5,5′-dithiobis (2-nitrobenzoic acid) (DTNB) as a thiol chromogenic probe. When V@Lipo (the Ce6-free version) was incubated with GSH at pH 6.5, a time- and temperature-dependent decrease in GSH content was observed. At 25°C, 39.60% of GSH remained after 6 hours, whereas at 37°C, only 9.71% of GSH persisted, indicating that physiological temperature accelerates VOx degradation and subsequent GSH depletion.83 This temperature dependence is particularly relevant for in vivo applications, as it ensures efficient GSH consumption under physiological conditions. VC@Lipo not only disrupts redox homeostasis but also enhances this effect through light-independent singlet oxygen (1O2) generation. As shown by Zhang et al using Singlet Oxygen Sensor Green (SOSG), the VOx nanozyme by itself can generate 1O2 when exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) in a mildly acidic environment.94 Recently, certain nanomaterials—including copper-based Cu-TCPP nanosheets, ultrathin manganese oxide (MnOx) nanosheets, and molybdenum-based CoMoO4-phosphomolybdic acid nanosheets—have been demonstrated to generate singlet oxygen (1O2) via the Russell mechanism, a process that operates independently of light irradiation.95 This mechanism, as described in the literature, involves the reaction of biological hydroperoxides in the presence of trace quantities of metal ions or enzymes, distinguishing it from photosensitizer-mediated 1O2 production, which requires both light and oxygen.96 The generation of 1O2 radicals was corroborated by ESR spectroscopy utilizing TEMP as a spin-trapping agent. Quantitative comparisons revealed that the photosensitizer Ce6 produced approximately 1.75-fold more 1O2 than the VOx nanozyme alone. Furthermore, when the VOx nanozyme was combined with the photodynamic effect of Ce6 under 660 nm laser irradiation, a synergistic enhancement in total ROS generation was observed. Quantitative assessment using 2,7-dichlorofluorescin diacetate (DCFH-DA) demonstrated that the VC@Lipo+H2O2+L treatment resulted in 16.88-fold higher ROS levels relative to the PBS control, substantially outperforming the single-treatment groups (4.65-fold for VC@Lipo+H2O2 and 7.99-fold for VC@Lipo+L).83

Flow cytometry showed VC@Lipo+L induced 48.74% apoptosis in 4T1 cells vs 25.27% (VC@Lipo) and 3.44% (laser only); live-dead staining confirmed extensive death in the combination group. GSH depletion reached 57.83% (VC@Lipo+L) vs 14.43% (V@Lipo) and 38.78% (C@Lipo+L), confirming redox disruption. JC-1 analysis revealed greatest mitochondrial damage in VC@Lipo+L (weaker red aggregates, brighter green monomers).94 By increasing ROS formation and simultaneously lowering endogenous antioxidant defenses, this dual-action method proves to be a very efficient approach for redox-based cancer treatment.81

A critical consideration for redox-responsive nanocarriers is the heterogeneity of glutathione levels across different tumor types, subtypes, and even within individual tumors. While many cancers exhibit elevated GSH concentrations (2–10 mM intracellularly) compared to normal tissues (1–2 mM), this is not universal. Tumors with low GSH levels—including certain breast cancer subtypes, some hematological malignancies, and early-stage lesions—may not provide sufficient redox differential to trigger effective drug release from GSH-responsive systems. Furthermore, intratumoral GSH heterogeneity, with higher levels in hypoxic regions and lower levels in well-perfused areas, can result in non-uniform drug release and incomplete tumor coverage. Acquired resistance to GSH-depleting therapies can also emerge through upregulation of glutathione synthesis enzymes (e.g, glutamate-cysteine ligase) or increased cystine uptake. These factors underscore the importance of patient stratification based on tumor GSH levels and the development of companion diagnostics to identify patients most likely to benefit from redox-responsive nanocarriers.91,93

The redox differential between tumor and normal tissues (GSH 2–10 mM vs 1–2 mM) is exploited by redox-responsive nanocarriers, but this strategy has important regenerative implications. First, glutathione plays a critical role in maintaining redox homeostasis in stem cell niches; excessive GSH depletion by redox-responsive carriers could impair hematopoietic stem cell self-renewal, mesenchymal stem cell osteogenic differentiation, and neural stem cell (NSC) proliferation.91 Second, while tumor cells exhibit elevated GSH, regenerating tissues also show increased GSH levels during active proliferation and matrix synthesis, potentially triggering off-target drug release at repair sites.93 Third, the wound healing environment is characterized by dynamic redox changes; the initial inflammatory phase involves ROS generation for bacterial clearance, followed by a shift toward reduced conditions (higher GSH) during proliferative and remodeling phases. Redox-responsive carriers activated by high GSH could therefore release drugs during the proliferative phase of wound healing, potentially disrupting angiogenesis, collagen deposition, and re-epithelialization.92 Fourth, acquired resistance to GSH-depleting therapies can arise through upregulation of glutamate-cysteine ligase; in the context of post-resection reconstruction, this could create a pro-recurrence niche by protecting residual tumor cells from therapy while promoting their survival and proliferation. Fifth, redox-responsive carriers may affect ECM remodeling, as MMPs require a reduced environment for optimal activity; GSH depletion could impair MMP-mediated ECM degradation essential for tissue repair and scaffold integration. These factors highlight the importance of patient stratification based on tumor GSH levels and the development of companion diagnostics to identify patients most likely to benefit from redox-responsive nanocarriers without compromising tissue repair.91

Enzyme-Responsive Systems
Nanocarriers engineered for enzyme responsiveness are designed to recognize and react to specific enzymes that are aberrantly overexpressed within the TME —including MMPs, cathepsin B, and hyaluronidase (HAase).97 These systems typically integrate enzyme-cleavable peptide sequences or polymeric frameworks that undergo hydrolytic degradation upon enzymatic cleavage, thereby effectuating targeted therapeutic release.

Enzyme-Triggered Release Systems
Several enzyme-triggered release systems have been developed to exploit the overexpression of tumor-associated proteases for targeted drug delivery and imaging. Cathepsin B-activatable photosensitizers have been developed by conjugating chlorin e4 to a folic acid quencher via an Arg-Arg-Lys (RRK) peptide linker, where cleavage by cathepsin B restores fluorescence and enables targeted PDT. Similarly, an AIEgen-based probe incorporating a Gly-Phe-Leu-Gly (GFLG) peptide linker enables cathepsin B-activatable fluorescence imaging (FI) and PDT.98,99

HAase, which degrades hyaluronic acid, is another key target. A graphene oxide-Ce6 complex coated with HA remains quenched until HAase hydrolyzes the HA shell, restoring fluorescence and singlet oxygen production for PDT.100 MMPs are targeted by a Cy5.5-labeled MMP-14-cleavable peptide conjugated to a GO-Au nanocomposite. Fluorescence recovers upon MMP-14 cleavage, while the Au nanoparticles enable highly effective photoacoustic imaging-guided PTT.101 Caspases, effectors of apoptosis, are used to monitor therapeutic response. A Pt (IV) prodrug with a caspase-3-cleavable DEVD peptide linked to an AIE fluorophore induces apoptosis and subsequent fluorescence activation for real-time monitoring of drug efficacy.102

Nanozymes: Enzyme-Mimetic Catalytic Systems
Nanomaterials endowed with enzyme-like catalytic properties—designated as nanozymes—have elicited substantial interest within the biomedical research community.103 These synthetic constructs confer multiple advantages relative to biological enzymes, including augmented catalytic turnover, economic production, robust operational stability, and susceptibility to external modulation via photonic, acoustic, or thermal stimuli.104 The progressive convergence of nanotechnology and biology has culminated in the widespread application of nanozymes across diverse biomedical domains, encompassing biosensing platforms, immunoassays, antibacterial interventions, and oncological therapeutics.105

Vanadium-based nanomaterials have demonstrated particular promise in enzyme-responsive contexts. Li and coworkers reported that V6O13, characterized by a staggered network architecture, manifests triple enzymatic activity—specifically oxidase, peroxidase, and catalase—rendering it suitable for fluorescence-based glucose, H2O2, and GSH sensing.61 Zeb et al contributed a rapid, single-pot synthetic route to mixed-valence VOx nanosheets for colorimetric detection of glucose and H2O2 via enzymatic cascade simulation.106 Ma and associates fabricated VOx nanodots through an ethanol-thermal approach, demonstrating dual POD- and CAT-mimetic activities alongside potent antibacterial efficacy via co-catalytic generation of superoxide and hydroxyl radicals.107 Beyond these specific nanomaterial systems, the bioactivity of diverse vanadium compounds—including oxidovanadium (IV) complexes (e.g, VOL), vanadium-flavonoid conjugates, vanadium pentoxide, and vanadyl sulfate—has been extensively investigated in relation to ROS production.108

The VOx nanozyme in the VC@Lipo system specifically demonstrates peroxidase-like activity, catalyzing the conversion of H2O2 to highly toxic •OH radicals through Fenton-like reactions.83 This intrinsic enzymatic activity contributes to its therapeutic effect independently of light, representing a form of enzyme-mimetic action within the broader context of TME-responsive nanocarriers. Nanocarriers that are activated by enzymes—specifically those containing peptides cleavable by cathepsin B—enable targeted release at desired sites. Quantitative measurements have shown that such systems deliver 5 to 10 times more of their therapeutic cargo in tumors with high protease activity. As an example, HA coatings that break down in the presence of HAase can expose hidden targeting ligands, which in turn increases cellular internalization by three times in cancers that overexpress CD44.97

Enzyme-responsive nanocarriers targeting MMPs, cathepsins, and HAase must consider the dual role of these enzymes in both tumor progression and tissue regeneration. MMPs are essential for ECM remodeling during wound healing and tissue repair, mediating collagen degradation, cell migration, angiogenesis, and stem cell recruitment. Nanoparticles that inhibit MMP activity to suppress tumor invasion could inadvertently impair regenerative processes, including scaffold degradation, neovascularization, and mesenchymal stem cell homing to injury sites. Conversely, MMP-responsive release of anti-cancer agents in regenerating tissues could occur due to physiological MMP upregulation during wound healing (MMP-1, MMP-2, MMP-9 are upregulated in the first 7–14 days post-injury), leading to off-target toxicity and delayed healing. Cathepsin B, while overexpressed in tumors, is also involved in bone resorption and cartilage remodeling; its inhibition for cancer therapy could affect skeletal regeneration, joint repair, and osteoarthritis progression. HAase-responsive systems must account for hyaluronic acid’s critical role in stem cell niche maintenance, tissue hydration, and cell migration during wound healing; premature degradation of HA-containing scaffolds could disrupt the regenerative microenvironment.97 Furthermore, TME is highly heterogeneous with respect to enzyme expression; some tumor regions may lack sufficient enzyme activity for effective drug release, while regenerating tissues may exhibit enzyme levels sufficient to trigger release.28 Multi-stimulus strategies (e.g, MMP + pH) can enhance selectivity by requiring multiple tumor-specific cues for activation, thereby reducing interference with physiological enzyme activity essential for tissue repair.81

Hypoxia-Responsive Systems
Tumor hypoxia—defined as oxygen tension below 1%—constitutes a defining feature of numerous solid malignancies, arising from a combination of insufficient vascular perfusion and elevated metabolic demand. Relative to healthy tissues, the TME displays several distinctive attributes, including reduced extracellular pH, elevated hydrogen peroxide and glutathione concentrations, and pronounced oxygen deprivation.109 Nanocarriers designed for hypoxia-responsive drug delivery commonly incorporate bioreducible functional groups—such as azobenzene, nitroimidazole, or quinone derivatives—which undergo reductive cleavage under hypoxic conditions, typically catalyzed by overexpressed reductase enzymes. The inherent susceptibility of azobenzene moieties to hypoxia-mediated scission facilitates the targeted release of nitroimidazole-based radiosensitizing agents, which augment radiotherapy efficacy by 2- to 3-fold, corresponding to a reduction in tumor volume of 70% as opposed to the 30% achieved in the absence of such sensitization.94

In response to endogenous tumor microenvironmental signals—particularly hypoxia (oxygen tension below 1%, compared with 5–10% in normal tissues)—nanozyme-based therapeutic platforms can exert site-specific catalytic activity. These systems either deplete factors that support malignant cell proliferation (e.g, glutathione, GSH) or generate cytotoxic species such as ROS, thereby suppressing cancer cell growth and potentiating oxidative stress-mediated apoptotic cell death.110 Although the VC@Lipo system does not incorporate specific hypoxia-responsive elements, the enhanced generation of 1O2 by the photosensitizer Ce6 under light irradiation is inherently oxygen-dependent, which highlights an important consideration for hypoxic tumor regions.111 The photodynamic effect requires molecular oxygen to generate singlet oxygen, and tumor hypoxia can therefore limit the efficacy of PDT. However, the VOx nanozyme component of VC@Lipo can generate 1O2 independently of light through its Russell-type mechanism, potentially offering an advantage in hypoxic conditions by maintaining ROS production even when oxygen is limited.112 This dual mechanism of ROS generation—light-dependent through Ce6 and light-independent through VOx—may help overcome the limitations imposed by tumor hypoxia, though dedicated hypoxia-responsive elements such as nitroimidazole-sensitized systems would be required for more direct targeting of this TME characteristic.82

While several nanozyme platforms have been described as “overcoming hypoxia” through oxygen-independent ROS generation, it is important to recognize the mechanistic limitations of this approach. First, the Russell mechanism for 1O2 generation from hydroperoxides, while oxygen-independent, requires the presence of biological hydroperoxides that may be limiting in severely hypoxic regions.96 Second, the Fenton-like reactions catalyzed by many nanozymes (e.g, VOx, MnO2, Cu-based systems) require H2O2 as a substrate; H2O2 concentrations in hypoxic tumors are often reduced due to diminished oxidative metabolism, potentially limiting •OH generation.83 Third, while some nanozymes can generate ROS independently of O2, the efficiency of these reactions is often lower than that of oxygen-dependent photosensitization or enzymatic catalysis, requiring higher nanozyme concentrations or combination strategies. Fourth, true “overcoming hypoxia” would require not only sustained ROS production but also alleviation of the broader consequences of hypoxia, including Hypoxia-Inducible Factor 1-Alpha (HIF-1α) stabilization, metabolic reprogramming, and immunosuppression.82 Therefore, a more accurate perspective is that oxygen-independent ROS generation represents a hypoxia-tolerant rather than hypoxia-overcoming strategy, and optimal approaches likely combine hypoxia-responsive drug release with oxygen-generating components (e.g, MnO2, catalase) that simultaneously alleviate hypoxic stress.109

Tumor hypoxia (O2 < 1%) arises from poor perfusion and high metabolic demand, providing a tumor-specific trigger for hypoxia-responsive nanocarriers. However, hypoxia is also a critical feature of regenerative microenvironments, particularly in bone healing, wound repair, and ischemic tissue recovery. HIF-1α stabilization during hypoxia promotes angiogenesis (via VEGF upregulation), stem cell recruitment (via SDF-1/CXCR4 signaling), and ECM synthesis essential for repair. Nanoparticles that release drugs in response to hypoxia could therefore activate in regenerating tissues, disrupting healing processes and potentially creating chronic wounds.109 Additionally, tumor hypoxia is highly heterogeneous, with well-perfused regions showing O2 > 5% and necrotic cores showing <0.5% O2; this heterogeneity can result in non-uniform drug release and incomplete tumor coverage, leaving residual tumor cells that may contribute to recurrence.113 While some nanozymes generate ROS independently of oxygen (e.g, VOx via Russell mechanism, certain MnO2-based systems), these reactions require hydroperoxides (e.g, H2O2) that may be limited in severely hypoxic regions due to diminished oxidative metabolism, reducing therapeutic efficacy.96 Furthermore, true “overcoming hypoxia” would require not only sustained ROS production but also alleviation of broader hypoxic consequences, including HIF-1α stabilization, metabolic reprogramming (shift to glycolysis), and immunosuppression (recruitment of MDSCs and Tregs).109 Optimal approaches combine hypoxia-responsive drug release with oxygen-generating components (e.g, MnO2, catalase, or perfluorocarbons) that simultaneously alleviate hypoxic stress while preserving regenerative angiogenesis and stem cell function.81 From a regenerative perspective, it is crucial to avoid complete elimination of hypoxia in the wound environment, as transient hypoxia is essential for initiating angiogenesis and stem cell recruitment during early repair phases.109

Multistimuli-Responsive Drug Delivery Systems (MSR-DDSs)
The rational design of MSR-DDSs necessitates a sequential, multi-stage strategy that addresses the significant biological barriers encountered between systemic administration and the final intracellular site of action. The journey begins with ensuring systemic circulation stability, where nanocarriers must evade rapid clearance by the mononuclear phagocyte system to maintain a prolonged half-life of 12–24 hours; this is typically achieved through surface modification with PEGylation, maintenance of a neutral surface charge, and optimization of a hydrodynamic diameter within the 50–150 nm range to circumvent renal filtration and splenic sequestration.68 Following successful circulation, the nanocarriers must exploit the EPR effect to extravasate from the tumor vasculature, a process that can be significantly augmented by active targeting ligands—such as RGD peptides, folate, or transferrin—which bind to overexpressed receptors on the tumor endothelium or stromal cells, thereby promoting selective tumor accumulation.64 However, accumulation alone is insufficient, as the dense stromal matrix and high interstitial fluid pressure of solid tumors impede further progress; this necessitates a third stage of deep tumor penetration, which is often enabled by an initial size reduction from approximately 100 nm to sub-20 nm particles or by a charge-switching mechanism, from a neutral or negative zeta potential to a positive one, triggered by specific TME signals such as acidic pH or overexpressed MMPs.114 Once the nanocarriers have successfully navigated the stromal barrier and reached the vicinity of parenchymal tumor cells, the fourth stage requires efficient cellular uptake, a process that is favored by a positive surface charge or by receptor-mediated endocytosis, frequently achieved via TME-induced charge reversal that optimizes interactions with the anionic cell membrane.115 Following internalization, the nanocarriers become entrapped within the acidic endosomal and lysosomal compartments (pH 4.5–5.5), presenting a critical bottleneck where payload degradation must be preempted; the fifth stage, endosomal escape, is therefore essential and can be accomplished through mechanisms such as the proton-sponge effect, the incorporation of membrane-disruptive peptides, or photochemical disruption to facilitate translocation into the cytosol.75 Finally, to realize their full therapeutic potential, the released drugs must reach their specific subcellular targets, a process requiring organelle-targeted release; this final stage is orchestrated by incorporating targeting signals, such as nuclear localization sequence (NLS) peptides for DNA-damaging agents or mitochondrial targeting moieties for pro-apoptotic drugs, coupled with stimuli-responsive release mechanisms that ensure the payload is unleashed only upon arrival at the designated organelle, thereby maximizing efficacy and minimizing off-target toxicity.29 Although single stimulus-responsive drug delivery systems (SSR-DDSs) have demonstrated utility in circumventing certain biological impediments to tumor drug delivery, their translational potential has been constrained by the inherent complexity and intratumoral heterogeneity characteristic of the TME, as well as the considerable variability observed across patient populations.116 A further complicating factor is that endogenous signals—such as acidic pH, enzyme overexpression, and reductive conditions—are not uniquely associated with neoplastic tissues and may be present in normal cells at varying levels, thereby increasing the risk of non-specific biodistribution and unintended toxicity.117 Externally applied stimuli, including light and magnetic fields, afford precise temporal and spatial control; however, their clinical applicability is limited by poor penetration depth. In response to these challenges, a new generation of carriers—MSR-DDSs—has been designed to integrate responsiveness to multiple cues. These advanced platforms are capable of executing sequential or simultaneous responses to diverse triggers, thereby facilitating the progressive overcoming of multiple physiological and pathological barriers that have traditionally limited effective cancer nanomedicine.5

Rational Design of MSR-DDSs to Overcome Sequential Barriers
An optimal drug delivery platform must be capable of sequentially surmounting multiple biological obstacles—including maintaining stability during systemic circulation, achieving tumor accumulation, penetrating into deep tumor parenchyma, facilitating cellular internalization, and escaping endosomal entrapment.118 (MSR-DDSs address these challenges by integrating multiple stimulus-activatable strategies within a single nanoplatform, enabling orchestrated responses to distinct triggers either sequentially or simultaneously to achieve sophisticated drug delivery.119

Stimulus-Induced Size-Reducible Nanocluster Strategy for Deep Penetration
A major hurdle in solid tumor therapy is the limited penetration of nanocarriers into deep tumor regions. While nanoparticles of approximately 100 nm are advantageous for prolonged circulation, they are impeded in their ability to penetrate deeply; conversely, particles smaller than 50 nm exhibit superior penetration but are subject to rapid clearance from circulation.114 The “cluster bomb” strategy reconciles the conflict between circulation stability and deep tumor penetration. Lei et al83 engineered pH-responsive nanoparticles that, upon encountering the acidic TME, undergo dissociation into two functional components: DOX-loaded mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) of approximately 100 nm for surface tumor cell ablation, and tLyP-1-modified WS2 quantum dots of <20 nm for deep tumor penetration and Near-Infrared (NIR)-mediated photothermal therapy. This dual-action system achieved a 93% tumor inhibition rate in vivo, markedly surpassing the efficacy of single-mechanism controls (approximately 70%).120,121

Response to Exogenous and Tumor Tissue Triggers
Combining exogenous stimuli (light, magnetic fields, ultrasound) with endogenous TME triggers enables treatment personalization and reduces individual variations. Exogenous stimuli act as a “switch” to seal nanoparticle pores preventing drug leakage, while endogenous triggers ensure targeted release within the tumor depth.122,123

“Heterostructure” nanoparticles (HSs), formed by connecting two or more inorganic nanoparticles with different functions, exemplify such systems. Kakwere et al used Au-FeₓOᵧ dimers as templates to prepare smart HSs with excellent heating performance in magnetic fields.124 Iron oxide in this structure serves as a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) agent and thermal medium for magnetism-induced hyperthermia, while the presence of gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) improves heat dissipation under alternating magnetic fields.125 A heat-responsive polymer, poly(N-isopropyl acrylamide) (PNIPAAM), was selectively connected to the gold domain for drug loading. Additionally, a pH-responsive polymer, poly(dimethylaminoethyl acrylate) (PDMAEA), was attached to the iron oxide surface for siRNA (Small Interfering RNA) delivery. Upon reaching the acidic TME, PDMAEA hydrolyzes, reversing its potential from positive to negative and releasing siRNA through polymer cleavage and charge repulsion. Conversely, at temperatures above the lower critical solution temperature (LCST, 43°C) generated by alternating magnetic fields, PNIPAAM undergoes conformational changes triggering payload release.126

Response to Exogenous and Cellular/Subcellular Triggers
Combining exogenous stimuli with cellular triggers (such as high glutathione levels) or subcellular triggers (such as endosome/lysosome pH) can enhance intracellular drug release and improve endosomal escape.38 Exogenous stimuli can remove the PEG layer from nanoparticle surfaces, increasing cellular uptake, while cellular stimuli induce size shrinkage and deep penetration.127,128

Gold nanorods (GNRs), owing to their unique high-efficiency photothermal conversion capability, provide an excellent platform for remotely controlled release of genetic agents based on light triggers. Wang et al constructed NIR/GSH-responsive AuNPs delivering p65-short hairpin shRNA (targeting nuclear factor-kappa B) for metastatic cancer treatment.5 Tumor-targeting RGD peptides were conjugated to Disulfide-linked Polyethylenimine (DSPEI) (a short Polyethylenimine (PEI) for gene therapy agent adsorption) via PEG spacers. GNRs were surface-functionalized with RGD-PEG-DSPEI segments through gold-mercaptan bonds for GSH response. A 2-nm polymer layer formed on the GNR surface with approximately 50 nm particle size. NIR laser irradiation and the “proton-sponge” effect of DSPEI facilitated endosomal/lysosomal escape after effective tumor cell uptake.127 Simultaneously, NIR-induced “hot” electron transfer and high intracellular GSH concentration reduced electrostatic adsorption of shRNAs and cleaved disulfide bonds, triggering shRNA release into the cytosol. Nanoparticles accumulated effectively in tumor tissue (12.3% of injected dose at 6 hours post-injection), and RDG/shRNA treatment with NIR irradiation reduced tumor volume by 83.5% compared to controls while significantly inhibiting pulmonary metastasis.129

Response to Tumor Tissue and Cellular/Subcellular Triggers
The effective delivery and biodistribution of therapeutic agents are substantially constrained by the inherent heterogeneity of tumor tissues, which is manifested through stromal cell proliferation, crosslinked extracellular matrix components, aberrant vascular architecture, and elevated interstitial hydrostatic pressure. To enhance nanoparticle delivery efficiency in solid malignancies, strategic modifications to particle size, morphology, or surface charge are being explored to circumvent these tissue-level obstacles. The TME —characterized by mildly acidic pH (6.5–7.2) and upregulated enzymatic activity—can be exploited to induce size reduction via de-PEGylation or nanoparticle disintegration, thereby facilitating penetration to varying tumor depths following EPR-mediated accumulation or ligand-directed targeting. Furthermore, nanoparticles incorporating ionizable groups can undergo charge reversal through protonation within the acidic TME, thereby augmenting cellular internalization.5,130

Size-Shrinkable Systems
Particle size critically affects biological distribution and tumor accumulation. Conventional nanoparticles (~100 nm) exhibit limited penetration into deep tumor regions owing to obstruction by dense stromal elements, whereas ultra-small nanoparticles (<30 nm) display enhanced interstitial transport and tumor infiltration but are compromised by poor tumor specificity and abbreviated circulation half-life.114 A dual-phase strategy has been proposed to reconcile these competing requirements. Yu et al developed a size-shrinkable carrier for doxorubicin delivery that integrates temperature, pH, and redox responsiveness to balance circulation stability with tumor penetrability. Mixed micelles comprising PNIPAM, 2-Hydroxyethyl Methacrylate (HEMA), Methacrylic Acid (MAA), and BACy were crosslinked via disulfide bonds. Disruption of the pH-sensitive MAA and thermoresponsive PNIPAM components induced volume contraction under tumor-mimetic pH and temperature conditions, promoting deeper tissue diffusion. Additionally, the disulfide linkages within BACy conferred reduction sensitivity to elevated intracellular GSH, accelerating DOX liberation following cellular uptake. Under simulated TME conditions, drug release reached 80% within 24 hours—substantially surpassing that achieved under single-stimulus conditions.131

Charge-Reversible Systems
Surface charge constitutes another critical determinant of tumor penetration, targeting efficiency, and cellular internalization. Cationic nanoparticles tend to aggregate with plasma proteins, adsorb to negatively charged normal cell membranes, and undergo recognition and clearance by the reticuloendothelial system.115 Accordingly, MSR-DDSs capable of switching surface charge—maintaining a negative or neutral charge during circulation and reverting to positive charge within the TME to facilitate cellular uptake—are highly desirable. Mo et al engineered charge-reversible zwitterionic oligopeptide liposomes (HHG2C18-L), composed of soy phosphatidylcholine and 1,5-dioctadecyl-glutamyl,2-histidyl-hexahydrobenzoic acid (HHG2C18), for mitochondrial targeting with multi-stage pH responsiveness. The synthetic lipid HHG2C18 comprises two stearyl alkane chains (hydrophobic blocks), a pH-cleavable hexahydrobenzamide group, and glutamic acid and histidine as hydrophilic moieties. The liposomal surface charge reversed to positive within the TME, promoting cellular uptake, while the proton-sponge effect and HHG2C18 hydrolysis generated a stronger positive charge following endosomal/lysosomal acidification. Zeta potential measurements revealed a value of −20 mV at pH 7.4, which shifted to +22 mV at pH 5.5 and +40 mV at pH 4.5, thereby enabling mitochondrial targeting through electrostatic interactions.132

Nuclear-Targeted Systems
The nucleus serves as a pharmacological target for numerous first-line chemotherapeutic agents. However, nanoparticle size imposes a constraint on nuclear delivery due to the nucleopore exclusion limit (<9 nm). While nanoparticles can be functionalized with NLS peptides to facilitate nuclear targeting, cationic NLS peptides often provoke non-specific tissue distribution and rapid clearance.29 Li et al designed polymer nanovesicles (PNVs) with multi-stage size and charge transitions to achieve enhanced nuclear accumulation. Each PNV, based on N-(2-hydroxypropyl) methacrylamide (HPMA), comprised two oppositely charged copolymers: an anionic HPMA conjugate decorated with 2,3-dimethylmaleic anhydride (P-DMA) and a cationic P-Dox R8NLS containing intracellularly detachable subgroups (IDSs). DOX was conjugated to the secondary targeting group R8NLS via hydrazone linkages. Acidic TME conditions induced charge reversal of P-DMA, resulting in PNV disassembly into linear conjugates—a first-stage size reduction from 55 nm to 10 nm—and exposure of R8 ligands to enhance internalization. Subsequent hydrazone bond cleavage within acidic lysosomes led to IDS degradation, a second-stage size contraction, and re-exposure of R8NLS, promoting nuclear-targeted DOX release and achieving 4.5-fold higher nuclear accumulation compared to DOX-loaded HPMA alone.44

MSR-DDSs for Combination Therapy Targeting Different Tumor-Associated Cells
Conventional anticancer agents primarily target tumor cells. However, cancer stem cells (CSCs) contribute to DNA repair and tumorigenesis, making combined inhibition of both tumor cells and CSCs a viable strategy. Liu et al prepared tumor-related stimuli-activated nanogels (aNG) using in situ interfacial polymerization for co-delivery of cytotoxic ribonuclease A (RNase A) and anti-CSC doxycycline (Doc) after overcoming sequential physiological barriers.133 aNG (~100 nm) was established as a core-shell polymer through hierarchical assembly. RNase A was first encapsulated in reduction-responsive single protein-based nanocapsules forming R-rNC (<10 nm) with positive surface potential for tumor perfusion and rapid release. A polymeric core formed by acrylamide, cationic monomer N-(3-aminopropyl) methacrylamide, azide-decorated monomer (AAm-N3), and acid-cleavable glycerol dimethacrylate (GDA) crosslinker loaded R-rNC and Doc. The polymeric core was shielded by dibenzocyclooctyne (DBCO) -modified HA conjugated to the azide group of AAm-N3, improving circulation and targeting ability.134 aNG collapsed under acidic conditions, dividing into Doc and R-rNC components that effectively targeted tumor cells and CSCs respectively. Small-sized R-rNC with positive surface charge were readily absorbed by tumor cells and biodegraded to release RNase A, while Doc eradicated CSCs by inhibiting mitochondrial biogenesis. These co-delivered agents synergistically reduced the average CD133+ subpopulation (TSC surface marker) from 10.5% to 0.69% and reduced tumor weight by 73.6% compared to controls.135,136

MSR-DDSs for Cancer Immunotherapy
Immunotherapy has emerged as a transformative approach in oncology, leveraging the host’s antitumor immune responses—a process that encompasses immune cell recognition, clonal expansion and activation, effector T cell trafficking and infiltration into neoplastic lesions, and ultimately targeted elimination of malignant cells while preserving healthy tissues.86 Despite the inherent potency of the human immune system, the TME deploys multiple evasion mechanisms, including immune checkpoint upregulation, polarization of macrophages toward pro-tumorigenic phenotypes, neutralization of cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes, and overexpression of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO). MSR-DDSs offer versatile platforms for the targeted or co-delivery of immunotherapeutic agents, while minimizing adverse autoreactive immune responses.137,138

Cheng et al developed sequence-responsive peptide-based nanoparticles for dual-targeted immunotherapy, achieving superior melanoma suppression with augmented cytotoxic T cell responses through simultaneous immune checkpoint blockade and IDO inhibition. Their system utilized amphiphilic DEAP- PD-1 Antagonist Peptide (DPPA-1)—comprising 3-diethylaminopropyl isothiocyanate (DEAP), an MMP-2-cleavable linker, and a Programmed Cell Death Protein 1 DPPA-1—to deliver the IDO inhibitor NLG919 as a co-assembly carrier. Protonation of the DEAP moiety in the acidic TME reduced hydrophobicity, inducing structural swelling; subsequent MMP-2-mediated cleavage triggered complete nanostructural disassembly and release of both DPPA-1 and NLG919 within the tumor stroma. NLG919@DEAP-DPPA-1 demonstrated potent antitumor activity and promoted CD8+ T cell differentiation.139

Immunologically “hot” tumors, characterized by robust T cell infiltration, generate effective antitumor immune responses, whereas “cold” tumors—which lack significant T cell presence—fail to elicit such responses.117 The conversion of cold tumors into immunogenic, proinflammatory phenotypes has become a cornerstone of contemporary immunotherapy. Several chemotherapeutic agents, including anthracyclines and oxaliplatin, induce immunogenic cell death (ICD) in cold tumors, releasing tumor antigens and thereby enabling antitumor immune responses and combination chemo-immunotherapy. Zheng et al synthesized folate-modified, monodispersed silica nanoparticles with pH- and GSH-responsive properties for targeted doxorubicin delivery, inducing ICD and maximizing immune activation. Intracellularly triggered DOX release induced apoptosis and high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) release, followed by antigen release from dying cells, which activated antigen-presenting cells and generated antitumor immune responses for subsequent tumor elimination.140,141

Exogenous photodynamic therapy (PDT) can also activate ICD. Hou et al induced ICD and promoted tumor-infiltrating cytotoxic T lymphocytes using PDT based on higher-order Boolean logic prodrug nanoparticles (BLPNs), which activated the photosensitizer pheophorbide a (PPa) and released NLG919 in response to intracellular redox conditions.42 The BLPN triggering strategy incorporated three elements: (i) MMP-2/9 cleavage of the PEG corona to enhance tumor accumulation and retention; (ii) degradation of disulfide bonds triggered by intracellular GSH to release NLG919; and (iii) protonation of acid-sensitive 2-(diisopropylamino)ethyl methacrylate to dissociate nanoparticles and activate pheophorbide a for PDT. PDT-induced tumor cell apoptosis, coupled with ICD generation, augmented tumor immunogenicity, while NLG919 inhibited IDO activity to prevent immune escape.142 Co-delivery of PPa and NLG919 synergistically modulated the tumor immune microenvironment, promoting both antitumor immunity and anti-immune escape, with elevated secretion of Interferon-Gamma (IFN-γ), Tumor Necrosis Factor-Alpha (TNF-α), and Interleukin-6 (IL-6) confirming the synergistic effects.42 In summary, the field has evolved from single-stimulus systems toward sophisticated MSR-DDSs. As summarized in Table 1, these platforms integrate diverse triggers—ranging from pH and redox to exogenous light—to sequentially overcome biological barriers such as deep tumor penetration and endosomal entrapment, while also providing critical context on their evidence level, safety profile, and translational challenges. This strategic layering of stimuli responsiveness is essential for achieving high therapeutic efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity. The sophisticated multistimuli-responsive platforms discussed above demonstrate notable precision in tumor targeting and drug release. However, their impact on shared pathways—Wnt, Notch, Hedgehog, and p53—remains largely unexplored. As these systems progress toward clinical translation, comprehensive pathway analysis will be essential to ensure that potent anticancer effects are not achieved at the expense of compromising regenerative capacity in healthy tissues.116 This consideration naturally leads to the next section, where biomimetic strategies offer a potential solution by mimicking native cellular interactions to achieve both targeting specificity and biological compatibility.

Regenerative Benefit versus Oncogenic Risk
Smart nanocarriers that exploit TME triggers (pH, redox, enzymes, hypoxia) achieve precise drug delivery and potent anti-tumor efficacy by suppressing oncogenic pathways (e.g, Wnt, Notch) within tumors. However, unintended inhibition of these same pathways in normal stem cell niches may impair tissue homeostasis and regenerative capacity, particularly in patients undergoing concurrent tissue repair or wound healing. Additionally, the immunomodulatory effects of certain nanocarriers may inadvertently create a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment if not precisely controlled. Future designs should incorporate pathway-selective, temporally controlled, and cell-type-specific release strategies to maximize anti-tumor efficacy while preserving regenerative potential in healthy tissues.

How Can Nanomaterials Simultaneously Promote Repair and Suppress Malignancy? Biomimetic and Cell-Membrane-Coated Nanocarriers
This section addresses the intersection of our central question: how nanoplatforms can simultaneously promote repair and suppress malignancy. We examine biomimetic and cell-membrane-coated nanocarriers that combine immune evasion, tumor targeting, and tissue-specific homing. These platforms offer a unique opportunity to achieve both therapeutic and regenerative outcomes within a single system, but their clinical translation is complicated by safety concerns that vary by membrane source—a critical consideration evaluated through the lens of “regenerative benefit versus oncogenic risk”.

Biomimetic Nanocarriers
Nanoparticles have attracted considerable interest as drug delivery platforms due to their favorable characteristics including stability, versatility in surface modification, and capacity to encapsulate therapeutic agents. These nano-sized carriers enable targeted drug delivery, reduce premature drug release, and provide sustained release profiles, ultimately extending circulation time and improving therapeutic outcomes. Nevertheless, nanoparticle-based delivery systems continue to face obstacles related to targeting precision and biological compatibility.143 Active targeting has been adopted to resolve targeting issues, using affinity ligands like aptamers, peptides, and antibodies on nanoparticle surfaces. To improve biocompatibility, protective polymer coatings are commonly applied to shield nanoparticles from immune attack. PEG polymers are particularly favored for their inertness, low cytotoxicity, and high biocompatibility. Conjugation with PEG notably decreases immunogenicity and increases systemic circulation half-life.144 However, investigations have demonstrated that repeated administration of PEGylated nanoparticles in animal models resulted in accelerated blood clearance and unfavorable biodistribution patterns. Consequently, alternative polymers including dextran, CS, polyvinyl pyrrolidone, and poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) have been investigated as stealth coatings.145

Among contemporary approaches for nanoparticle surface engineering, biomimetic strategies have gained considerable momentum owing to their inherent biocompatibility and immune-evasive properties, inspired by the principle of emulating biological systems.143 This biomimetic approach produces cancer cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (CCm@NPs) with a core–shell structure (nanoparticle core—liposomes, inorganic particles, or polymers—enveloped by a natural cell membrane), enabling them to mimic endogenous entities and evade reticuloendothelial clearance.70 Moreover, cell membranes derived from diverse cellular sources confer distinct biological functionalities upon the coated nanoparticles. For instance, neutrophil membrane-coated nanoparticles exhibit tropism toward inflammatory sites, while CCm@NPs demonstrate homotypic binding to source tumor cells.37,146 The biological functions of cell membranes—including immune evasion, prolonged circulation, and receptor-mediated targeting—have been systematically harnessed to develop biomimetic nanocarriers for tumor theranostics. Recent comprehensive reviews have extensively summarized the design principles, functionalization strategies, and imaging applications of cell membrane-coated nanoparticles, highlighting their potential to overcome the limitations of conventional synthetic nanocarriers.147

Classification of Cell Membrane-Coated Nanoparticles
CMC@NPs are classified according to the cellular origin of their membrane coatings into several categories: red blood cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (RBCm@NPs), platelet membrane-coated nanoparticles (PLTm@NPs), white blood cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (WBCm@NPs), stem cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (SCm@NPs), CCm@NPs, and hybrid membrane-coated nanoparticles (Hym@NPs).147

The first CMC@NPs were constructed using erythrocyte membranes. In 2011, Hu et al148 successfully fabricated RBCm@NPs via a top-down approach involving co-extrusion of PLGA nanoparticles with pre-formed RBC membrane-derived vesicles. These biomimetic particles achieved a circulation half-life of 39.6 hours, markedly surpassing the 15.8-hour half-life of PEGylated counterparts. In 2013, Parodi and coworkers149 advanced the field by developing WBCm@NPs through coating nanoporous silicon particles with leukocyte-derived membranes. Their studies demonstrated that WBCm@NPs exhibited diminished phagocytic uptake, enhanced adhesion to inflamed endothelium, and improved tumor accumulation. Building on these foundations, Hu’s laboratory introduced PLTm@NPs in 2015,150 integrating platelet membranes with doxorubicin-loaded nanogels for breast cancer applications; these constructs displayed extended circulation and potent tumor-homing capabilities. In 2016, Rao et al151 developed CCm@NPs by cloaking upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) with cancer cell membrane-derived vesicles for theranostic applications, uniquely combining homologous tumor targeting with immune evasion. Concurrently, Gao and coworkers152 introduced SCm@NPs, employing stem cell membranes to encapsulate doxorubicin-loaded gelatin nanogels, thereby enhancing chemotherapeutic efficacy with pronounced tumor affinity and reduced reticuloendothelial clearance. A landmark contribution came in 2017 when Dehaini et al153 introduced Hym@NPs by fusing RBC and platelet membranes to coat PLGA nanoparticles, yielding constructs that retained characteristics of both parental cell types.

Beyond these established membrane sources, unconventional options have emerged, including bacterial membranes, viral-mimetic membranes, neural cell membranes, and fibroblast cell membranes.154,155 These innovations continue to expand the biomimetic nanoparticle design space.

Preparation of Cell Membrane-Coated Nanoparticles
The fabrication of cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (CMC@NPs) predominantly relies on top-down methodologies. The process commences with the isolation of cell membranes, during which harvested cells are subjected to membrane disruption via hypotonic lysis,156 mechanical homogenization,157 or repeated freeze–thaw cycles.158 Subsequent differential centrifugation removes intracellular components, yielding membrane fragments. These fragments may then be processed into uniformly sized vesicles through extrusion across polycarbonate membranes. The resultant fragments or vesicles are subsequently applied to nanoparticle surfaces utilizing co-extrusion, sonication, or microfluidic electroporation. Additionally, spontaneous membrane coating can occur through electrostatic interactions between charged nanoparticles and membrane vesicles.159

Co-Extrusion Method
Co-extrusion constitutes a prevalent methodology for the fabrication of cell membrane-coated nanoparticles, wherein membrane-derived vesicles and nanoparticle cores are sequentially extruded through polycarbonate membranes of progressively diminishing pore dimensions. This mechanical processing induces conformational reorganization of the membrane bilayer and its subsequent deposition onto nanoparticle surfaces. The resulting CMC@NPs are characterized by a homogeneous size distribution and preserve both the structural integrity and functional activity of membrane-associated proteins. This approach has been exemplified by the work of Li and associates, who fabricated RBCm@NPs via co-extrusion of Ag2S quantum dot cores with erythrocyte membrane vesicles. Notwithstanding its extensive utilization in academic research, the scalability of co-extrusion for industrial production is constrained by its intrinsically labor-intensive and time-consuming procedural requirements.41

Sonication Method
Sonication offers a more straightforward and time-efficient alternative to co-extrusion, employing ultrasonic waves to fuse membrane vesicles with nanoparticle cores. Chen et al160 employed sonication to coat mesoporous silica-coated bismuth nanorods with platelet membranes. In comparative studies by Cai et al,161 Hym@NPs fabricated via sonication demonstrated enhanced stability and reduced dimensions relative to those produced through co-extrusion. Achieving uniform coating necessitates optimization of multiple parameters including amplitude, frequency, and duration. Moreover, careful monitoring of potential temperature elevation during sonication is essential to prevent denaturation of membrane proteins.

Microfluidic Electroporation Method
Since the initial demonstration of its conceptual feasibility in 2001, microfluidic electroporation has commanded escalating research interest. Microfluidic chips specifically designed for electroporation afford enhanced transfection efficiencies whilst operating at diminished voltage requirements.162 These microfluidic platforms are equipped with dual inlet ports that facilitate the simultaneous introduction and homogeneous mixing of nanoparticle suspensions and membrane preparations within the microchannel network. Upon traversal of the electroporation zone, the application of electrical pulses induces transient membrane permeabilization, permitting nanoparticle translocation; the resultant CMC@NPs are subsequently harvested at the device outlet.163 In a notable application, Wu and associates164 employed electrophoresis-based microfluidic chips to deposit neutrophil-derived vesicle coatings onto magnetic nanoparticles. This methodology enables high-throughput fabrication of CMC@NPs with superior encapsulation efficiency and stability.165 Notwithstanding the associated economic considerations, microfluidic electroporation holds substantial potential for real-world translation.

Application of Cell Membrane-Coated Nanoparticles in Cancer Treatment
Over the past decade, CMC@NPs have been investigated across diverse anti-tumor strategies, demonstrating substantial therapeutic potential. This section elucidates the properties and mechanisms of various CMC@NP classifications and presents recent advances in tumor therapy.

Red Blood Cell Membrane-Coated Nanoparticles
Erythrocytes—the most prevalent cellular constituents of blood—are primarily tasked with oxygen transport and are characterized by an extended circulatory lifespan of approximately 120 days. The exploration of erythrocytes as carriers for bioactive compounds was initiated in early studies,166 and a landmark contribution by Hu et al148 introduced the isolation of RBCm for biomimetic coating applications. The abundant availability of membrane material is underscored by the presence of roughly 5 billion red blood cells per milliliter of blood, a supply further facilitated by the absence of a nucleus and complex intracellular organelles in these cells.

RBCm represent particularly promising biomimetic materials for extending nanoparticle residence time in circulation. This advantage derives from “self-marker” proteins expressed on the membrane surface that enable immune evasion. CD47 serves as a critical marker interacting with the inhibitory receptor Signal-Regulatory Protein Alpha (SIRPα) expressed on macrophages, functioning as a “do not eat me” signal that protects RBCm@NPs from phagocytic clearance.167 Based on their immune-evasive properties and prolonged circulation, RBCm@NPs have been extensively investigated for anti-tumor drug delivery. However, clinical translation remains constrained by limited tumor-targeting capability.70 To overcome the inherent targeting limitations of native RBCm-coated nanocarriers, recent advances have focused on the functional redesign of erythrocyte-based nanomedicine through diverse surface engineering strategies. As comprehensively reviewed by Sun et al, the re-functionalization of erythrocyte-based platforms has been systematically categorized into five principal approaches: (i) lipid insertion—enabling the physical incorporation of ligand–linker–lipid conjugates (e.g, DSPE-PEG-folate, DSPE-PE G-maleimide) into the RBC membrane bilayer without disrupting existing surface proteins; (ii) biotin–avidin bridges—leveraging the strongest known non-covalent interaction (Kd ≈ 10−15 M) for indirect conjugation of targeting ligands, imaging agents, or nanoparticles onto RBC m; (iii) 1-Ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)carbodiimide (EDC)/ N-Hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) coupling—facilitating covalent attachment of carboxyl-bearing molecules to amine groups on RBCm for stable conjugation; (iv) antibody/ligand–receptor conjugation—enabling both ex vivo and in vivo functionalization through binding to RBC surface proteins such as glycophorin A, band 3, or complement receptor 1; and (v) passive adsorption (hitchhiking)—utilizing electrostatic or hydrophobic interactions for temporary cargo attachment with shear stress-triggered release. These re-functionalization strategies have transformed erythrocyte-based nanomedicine from passive long-circulating carriers into actively targeted, multifunctional theranostic platforms capable of integrating chemotherapy, immunotherapy, photodynamic therapy, photothermal therapy, and diagnostic imaging within a single system.30 This paradigm shift has significantly enhanced the delivery efficiency of RBCm-coated nanoparticles to tumor sites, addressing the critical limitation of poor active targeting that has historically constrained their clinical translation. Among these strategies, the lipid insertion approach has been particularly widely adopted due to its simplicity, mild reaction conditions, and minimal disruption of membrane proteins. Fang and colleagues168 proposed a lipid insertion strategy to enhance tumor-targeting efficiency of cell membrane-based nanoparticles while preserving protein biodistribution, wherein targeting ligands including folic acid, tumor-homing peptides, or neurotoxin-derived peptides are incorporated as ligand-linker-lipid conjugates via lipid tethers.

Immunotherapy suppresses tumor progression by restoring normal immune responses, and combination with chemotherapy demonstrates enhanced anticancer efficacy. Curdlan, a linear β-glucan, activates macrophage receptors inducing pro-inflammatory cytokine production112 and promotes polarization of tumor-associated macrophages toward inflammatory phenotypes.169 Low molecular weight curdlan served as an immunomodulatory carrier in research by Lin and coworkers, who engineered RBCm-coated lCUR loaded with doxorubicin for melanoma therapy (lCUR-DOX@RBC). Assessment of immune evasion capability through incubation with bone marrow-derived macrophages revealed minimal fluorescence in lCUR-DOX@RBC-treated samples, indicating reduced macrophage uptake. In vivo studies demonstrated that lCUR-DOX@RBC achieved prolonged circulation and significantly enhanced tumor growth inhibition following 12-day treatment.170 Of note, while this platform shows promise for melanoma therapy, its evaluation has been confined to tumor suppression models and has not yet incorporated wound healing or tissue repair components—a critical gap for theragenerative applications.

Non-invasive oncological modalities—including photodynamic therapy and photothermal therapy—have garnered considerable interest owing to their versatility and straightforward application.88 Among photothermal agents, melanin has emerged as a particularly attractive candidate, distinguished by its exceptional light-to-heat conversion efficiency.143 Zhang and colleagues.171 Zhang and colleagues172 extracted melanin nanoparticles from human black hair and employed them for photothermal ablation of hepatocellular carcinoma. To optimize their pharmacokinetic profile, these melanin nanoparticles were further functionalized with cRGD peptides via lipid insertion and subsequently cloaked with red blood cell membranes (yielding HNP@RBCm-cRGD). This biomimetic coating strategy effectively prolonged circulation time and augmented tumor accumulation, while preserving the intrinsic photothermal conversion performance of the melanin core.

Platelet Membrane-Coated Nanoparticles (PLTm@NPs)
Platelets originate from cytoplasmic fragmentation of mature megakaryocytes and represent the smallest blood cells. Despite their small size, platelets possess complete membrane structures while lacking nuclei, facilitating PLTm isolation. Similar to RBCm@NPs, CD47 protein expression on PLTm coatings contributes to evasion of phagocytic recognition. Additionally, PLTm express diverse functional antigens, receptors, and proteins including CD55, CD59, P-selectin, and glycoprotein Ib, which participate in tumor targeting, metastasis, bacterial infection, and thrombosis.173

Bahmani and colleagues174 developed polylactic acid (PLA) cores encapsulating resiquimod (R848), a Toll-like receptor agonist, subsequently coated with PLTm to exploit platelet membrane affinity for cancer cells within the TME. PLTm@NPs possess the capacity to respond to thrombotic signals that recruit platelets. This observation inspired Wang and coworkers175 to develop a strategy utilizing targeted coagulation for navigation of drug delivery to tumor sites. They engineered a fusion protein comprising truncated tissue factor and Arg-Gly-Asp peptide (tTF-RGD) as a coagulation cascade initiator, along with anti-PD-1 antibody-conjugated platelets (P-aPD-1) responsive to coagulation signals. Following intravenous or peritumoral tTF-RGD administration, enhanced coagulation signals at tumor sites recruited P-aPD-1. Activated platelets subsequently released platelet-derived microparticles and discharged aPD-1 antibodies to reactivate T cells.

PLTm@NPs have been employed for delivery of photosensitizers and photothermal agents. Xu and colleagues176 applied PLTm coatings to photosensitizer (verteporfin)-loaded PLGA nanoparticles (NP-Ver@P). These coated nanoparticles exhibited significantly enhanced tumor uptake compared to RBCm-coated counterparts while maintaining comparable systemic circulation. Subsequent research by Ning and coworkers177 engineered platelet vesicles containing Cu2O nanoparticles encapsulating aggregation-induced emission photosensitizer (TBP-2), achieving prolonged circulation and improved tumor targeting. Their cuproptosis-sensitizing system triggered multiple tumor cuproptosis induction events, effectively suppressing breast cancer lung metastasis in both cellular and murine models.

White Blood Cell Membrane-Coated Nanoparticles
Leukocytes play essential roles in pathogen recognition, elimination, and immune system regulation, maintaining physiological homeostasis. These cells migrate toward inflammatory sites in response to chemokine gradients. Given that chronic inflammation characterizes many cancers with associated chemokine overexpression, WBCm@NPs demonstrate targeted accumulation in tumor tissues.178 Furthermore, immune recognition proteins expressed on WBCm can engage with cancer cell surface molecules, enabling precise site-specific targeting. Additionally, WBCm-camouflaged nanoparticles evade immune detection. These properties establish WBCm@NPs as promising anticancer delivery systems, encompassing neutrophil membrane-coated nanoparticles (Nm@NPs), macrophage membrane-coated nanoparticles (Mm@NPs), T cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (Tm@NPs), dendritic cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (DCm@NPs), and natural killer cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (Natural Killer Cell Membrane (NKm)@NPs).179

paper.title: From smoke to stemness: Mechanisms of cancer stem cell induction by cigarette smoke.
paper.journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Reviews on cancer
paper.abstract: Cigarette smoking remains a dominant, preventable driver of cancer morbidity and mortality, and clinical outcomes in smokers remain disproportionately poor even with targeted and immune therapies. Beyond mutagenesis, cigarette smoke (CS) remodels cell state by promoting stem-like programs and enriching cancer stem cells (CSCs), a subpopulation with self-renewal capacity and therapy resistance that drives tumor heterogeneity, metastasis, and treatment failure. CS activates stemness-linked pathways, including Wnt/β-catenin, Notch, Hedgehog/GLI, NF-κB, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and TGF-β, and remodels the tumor microenvironment to further support CSC properties. While CS effects on lung tissue are well documented, its role in CSC induction at distant organs remains less understood. In this narrative, mechanistically organized review, we examine in vitro, in vivo, and clinical evidence linking CS exposure to CSC induction in primary lung cancer and secondary cancers at distant sites. We propose a unifying framework in which CS acts as a stemness-conditioning exposure that couples oncogenic signaling, epigenetic rewiring, and microenvironmental remodeling to stabilize therapy-evasive CSC states, converging on shared endpoints across tissues via tissue-specific intermediate signaling, and highlight therapeutic vulnerabilities arising from this framework.

paper.title: Redox Rewiring in Nicotine-Driven Gastric Carcinogenesis: Uncovering ROS-Dependent Oncogenic Circuits.
paper.abstract:
SIGNIFICANCE: Nicotine from tobacco products, secondhand smoke, and emerging delivery systems remains a major but underappreciated driver of gastric carcinogenesis (GC). Although reactive oxygen species (ROS) have long been implicated in tumor biology, current models incompletely explain how chronic nicotine selectively reprograms gastric epithelial signaling. This review advances the concept of redox rewiring, whereby nicotine establishes a persistent oxidative state that orchestrates multiple oncogenic programs via spatially compartmentalized NOX signaling.

RECENT ADVANCES: We synthesize evidence for a unified model wherein nicotine activates nAChR/β-AR signaling, Ca2+ influx, PKC, and compartmentalized NOX-derived ROS to generate distinct oncogenic outputs. Beyond the established NOX/ROS/NF-κB/MAPK-driven IL-8 and MMP-9 axes, we integrate emerging evidence into three interconnected modules governing EMT/metastasis (ABL1/STAT3/COX-2/periostin), survival/chemoresistance (ERK/GLI1/Bcl-2), and invasion/immune evasion (miR-21/PDCD4). Collectively, these circuits suggest that ROS function not merely as damaging byproducts but as spatially organized signaling mediators dictating tumor behavior.

CRITICAL ISSUES: A major challenge is distinguishing established mechanisms from incompletely validated models. The three proposed axes are testable hypotheses requiring experimental validation. Most data derive from in vitro studies with nonphysiologic nicotine concentrations, and artifacts from nonspecific ROS probes are common. Compensatory pathway activation and multi-target effects of natural products remain underexplored.

FUTURE DIRECTIONS: We outline a precision-redox oncology roadmap linking pathway-specific biomarkers, mechanistically matched natural products, and biomarker-enriched trials. Priorities include genetic validation of the three axes, time-resolved ROS imaging, and pulsed natural product regimens. By reframing nicotine-driven GC as adaptive redox network remodeling, this review provides a framework for prevention, stratification, and next-generation therapy. Antioxid.
